title: Digital Transformation and Corporate ESG Performance: A Literature Review on Mechanisms of Action
summary: Digital transformation has also become one of the most important drivers of the sustainable development of enterprises under the influence of the digital economy. Being an assessment tool that assesses the overall performance of enterprises in environmental, social responsibility, and corporate governance, ESG has gained popularity among scholars and practitioners alike. Even though an increasing body of literature investigates the effect of digital transformation on corporate ESG performance, the results regarding the main effect have been inconclusive, and additional research on transmission paths and boundary conditions is possible. In accordance with the literature-review methodology, this paper selects appropriate articles in the CNKI and Web of Science databases published in 20182025. It summarizes the present studies along three dimensions: main effect, mediating transmission paths, and moderating boundary conditions, examines the reasons behind empirical divergences, identifies the gaps in research, and gives the directions to be followed in future research. The research reveals that digital transformation influences corporate ESG performance mostly via three channels: resource allocation, internal governance, and green innovation, and that these effects are conditioned by various internal and external variables. Most of the available research works center their attention on major A-share listed companies, whereas the mechanisms of testing small- and medium-sized companies require further study. This paper will serve as the basis of further empirical research and the practice of coordinated digital-green development in enterprises.

title: Digital transformation and corporate ESG performance: green technological innovation, market concentration, and the twin transformation perspective
summary: This study examines whether, how, and under what market-structure conditions corporate digital transformation improves environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance. Building on the twin green and digital transformation perspective, this study conceptualizes digital transformation as a dynamic green digital capability rather than merely the adoption of digital technologies. By integrating the Natural Resource-Based View, Stakeholder Theory, and the Porter Hypothesis, we develop a framework in which digital transformation enhances ESG performance by strengthening firms’ data-driven sustainability capabilities and enabling green technological innovation. Using panel data from Chinese A-share listed firms from 2009 to 2023, we find that digital transformation is positively associated with ESG performance, measured by Huazheng ESG ratings. Green technological innovation mediates this relationship, and the empirical results indicate that the mediation is partial and economically modest, suggesting that green innovation is only one mechanism within a broader set of digitalization–ESG channels. Market concentration strengthens the positive effect of digital transformation on ESG performance, indicating that firms in more concentrated industries are better able to appropriate returns from long-term digital and sustainability investments. Additional heterogeneity analyses show that the positive effect of digital transformation is observed across regions and ownership types. In pollution-related industry subsamples, the effect is significant among non-high-polluting firms but not statistically significant among high-polluting firms; however, the between-group difference is not statistically significant. This study contributes to the literature by clarifying the innovation mechanism and market-structure boundary condition through which digital transformation supports comprehensive ESG improvement. The findings suggest that the ESG value of digital transformation depends not only on whether firms adopt digital technologies, but also on whether they develop dynamic green digital capabilities and operate in market environments that support long-term sustainability investment.

title: Can Independent Directors with Industry Managerial Experience More Effectively Curb Corporate Greenwashing? Evidence from Chinese Listed Companies
summary: In sustainable finance practices, greenwashing behavior of listed companies can trigger misallocation and inefficient delivery of financial services. Furthermore, if greenwashing is not promptly contained, it may incentivize firms to carry out environmentally destructive activities, which is harmful to environmental protection and sustainable economic development. In this context, we empirically study the effect of independent directors’ industry managerial experience on the greenwashing behavior of Chinese listed companies based on 15,107 firm-year observations of Chinese A-share listed companies from 2008 to 2024. We find a significant negative association between independent directors’ industry managerial experience and corporate greenwashing. Our evidence suggests that industry managerial experience of independent directors is a governance attribute with potential monitoring value for mitigating greenwashing.

title: Digital Transformation in Agri-Food Supply Chains for Adaptive Sustainable Growth among Latin American Firms: A Systematic Review, 2018–2025
summary: Background Digital transformation is reshaping agri-food supply chains through technologies designed to improve efficiency, traceability, sustainability, and resilience. However, the evidence remains fragmented, and Latin America continues to be underrepresented. Methods A systematic review complemented by bibliometric analysis was conducted using Scopus and Web of Science in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. The search identified 2,553 records; after filtering, duplicate removal, and eligibility assessment, 85 studies were included in the systematic synthesis. Data were analyzed using Bibliometrix, VOSviewer, and Microsoft Excel. Results Scientific output increased steadily, particularly after 2021. Blockchain, the Internet of Things, big data, artificial intelligence, and precision agriculture were the most frequently studied technologies. The findings showed improvements in traceability, operational efficiency, resource management, resilience, and organizational capabilities. Nevertheless, persistent barriers included inadequate infrastructure, limited financing, poor interoperability, and gaps in digital skills. Latin America accounted for only a small share of the scientific literature. Conclusions Digital transformation can support the sustainable growth of agri-food firms when it is integrated with organizational capabilities, data governance, stakeholder collaboration, and inclusive technology policies. Further empirical evidence from Latin America is needed, together with models tailored to the characteristics of its firms and territories.

title: The Rise of Neo Banks and Virtual Banking in the Digital Economy
summary: Abstract The global banking sector is undergoing a profound transformation driven by rapid digitalization, financial technology (FinTech) innovations, and changing consumer expectations. Neo banks and virtual banking institutions have emerged as significant disruptors, offering branchless, technology-driven, and customer-centric financial services. This paper examines the rise of neo banks and virtual banking in the digital economy with a special focus on India. Using secondary data and analytical methods, the study evaluates growth trends, technological foundations, impact on traditional banking, financial inclusion outcomes, and regulatory challenges. The findings indicate that neo banks enhance operational efficiency, customer convenience, and access to finance, particularly for millennial, small businesses, and underserved populations. However, issues related to cybersecurity, regulatory clarity, and sustainable profitability remain key challenges. The paper concludes with policy and strategic suggestions for strengthening neo banking ecosystems in the digital economy.

title: Explaining green finance scarcity and uneven distribution across Sub-Saharan Africa
summary: Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) is among the regions least responsible for historical greenhouse gas emissions yet faces some of the most severe consequences of climate change, and green capital flows to the region remain small relative to need. This article asks why green finance in SSA has remained geographically concentrated and structurally shallow despite widespread climate-financing needs across the region. It addresses this question through a structured narrative review with comparative case analysis, synthesizing evidence from institutional reports, multilateral datasets and peer-reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2026, identified through searches of Scopus, Web of Science and EconLit, supplemented by the AfDB, World Bank, OECD, Climate Policy Initiative (CPI) and IFC repositories using combinations of the terms “green finance,” “climate finance,” “Sub-Saharan Africa,” “green bonds” and related terms (full protocol in Sect. 3). The review is organized around an integrated conceptual framework that links market failure, development finance, and institutional and sustainable finance theory to a single causal chain running from climate-finance need to green investment outcomes. It is illustrated with four contrasting country cases (South Africa, Kenya, Nigeria, Ethiopia) selected to vary systematically in capital-market depth, regulatory maturity, and private-sector development. The synthesis indicates that green finance instruments—green bonds, climate funds, blended finance, and sustainability-linked loans—have gained traction, but that flows remain dominated by public capital and are concentrated in a handful of more financially developed economies. The evidence points to five interacting constraints—financial-system shallowness, macroeconomic and currency risk, regulatory and taxonomy gaps, data asymmetries, and institutional capacity limitations—and suggests that closing the gap requires harmonized regulatory frameworks, systematic de-risking, local capital-market deepening, and stronger climate-risk supervision, sequenced against each country’s specific constraint profile rather than applied uniformly. By identifying the specific financial, regulatory, and institutional levers that would unlock green capital, the article provides policy-relevant insights for advancing the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 7 (affordable and clean energy), SDG 9 (industry, innovation and infrastructure), SDG 13 (climate action), and SDG 17 (partnerships for the goals). It clarifies what mobilizing climate finance at scale would mean for SSA’s broader progress on poverty (SDG 1) and inclusive economic growth (SDG 8).

title: FINANCIAL PERFORMANCE: GOVERNANCE, RISK, COMPLIANCE AND DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION
summary: The disparity between aggregate banking profitability and individual bank performance, coupled with inconclusive evidence on Governance, Risk, Compliance, and Digital Transformation, necessitates further investigation. The study aims at examining their effects on the financial performance of conventional commercial banks listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange during 2020–2024. Using 80 firm-year observations, this study employs a Random Effects Model with cluster-robust standard errors. Financial performance is measured by Return on Assets (ROA), while Governance is represented by the Board of Directors, Audit Committee, and Independent Board of Commissioners; Risk by the Non-Performing Loan (NPL) ratio; Compliance by a Compliance Disclosure Index based on GRI Standards 2021; and Digital Transformation by a Digital Transformation Index. The results show that NPL and Digital Transformation negatively affect ROA, while Governance, Compliance, CAR, and OEtOI have no significant effects. The study provides an integrated assessment of these factors in Indonesian banking.

title: When Firms Lead States: Financial Intermediaries and the Politics of Sovereign Green Bond Issuance
summary: Abstract Sovereign green bonds typically appear only after corporate green bond issuance has accumulated—a sequence at odds with the policy consensus that sovereign borrowing anchors debt market development. I argue that the inversion reflects market building by global investment banks. The four banks that authored the Green Bond Principles in 2014 used early private corporate transactions to build the verification practices, pricing conventions, and investor networks needed for a functioning market, then served as lead managers when sovereigns entered, transferring accumulated expertise across the public–private divide. States entered a market whose institutional infrastructure they did not design. The Cox proportional hazards model shows that accumulated corporate issuance significantly accelerates sovereign entry, while government agency issuance delays it by substituting for direct sovereign participation. A bank-level triangulation shows that founding-bank presence at sovereign entry reflects green-bond-specific expertise transfer rather than general dominance in sovereign debt underwriting. The findings identify financial intermediaries as a distinct channel through which sustainable finance reaches sovereign borrowers and show how privately constructed market conditions shape the terms on which states engage with global climate finance.

title: Managing the Green Economy through Digital Technologies: Opportunities, Mechanisms, and Prospects
summary: This article analyzes the theoretical and methodological foundations, practical mechanisms, and prospects of managing the green economy through digital technologies. The interrelationship between the green economy and digital transformation is examined from the perspective of the "twin transition." The study substantiates the role of artificial intelligence, Big Data, the Internet of Things (IoT), and blockchain technologies in improving energy efficiency, tracking carbon footprints, managing waste, and shaping green finance flows, and proposes institutional mechanisms for their governance. Drawing on a comparative analysis of international experience (the European Union, China, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom, and Singapore) and Uzbekistan's practice, supported by official statistical data, the authors develop an original conceptual model, the "digital-green governance cycle," together with practical recommendations for managing the digital-green transition in Uzbekistan. The research methodology combines systems analysis, a comparative-historical approach, and the generalization of statistical data.

title: Exploring the impact of corporate governance and external audit quality on creative accounting practices
summary: The current study adopts a multivariate model to investigate the impact of board size, board independence, managerial ownership, audit committee independence, and external audit quality (proxied by audit fees) on creative accounting practices. Data for the study were obtained from commercial banks’ annual reports published on the Amman Stock Exchange (ASE) during the period from 2017 to 2021. The results of the ordinary least squares (OLS) regression analysis reveal that managerial ownership and audit fees have a significant positive impact on creative accounting, while audit committee independence has a significant negative impact. In addition, the results reveal that neither board independence nor board size influences creative accounting. The study findings highlight the need for effective regulatory oversight and monitoring of the extent of managerial ownership and audit fees to curb earnings management practices. In addition, the findings accentuate the importance of audit committee independence for enhancing financial reporting quality and integrity within the banking sector. The study concludes with several recommendations that hopefully enhance transparency and the quality of financial reporting in the banking sector.

title: DOES CHIEF AUDIT EXECUTIVE TENURE AFFECT CEO OVERCONFIDENCE IN REAL EARNINGS MANAGEMENT?
summary: CEO overconfidence tends to make high-risk decisions, including engaging in real earnings management (REM); however, the role of Chief Audit Executive (CAE) tenure as a governance mechanism that may moderate this relationship remains underexplored. This study aims at examining the effect of CEO overconfidence on REM and the moderating role of CAE tenure in this relationship. The sample consists of manufacturing companies listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) during the 2012–2019 period and was analyzed using a fixed-effects panel data regression model. The results showed that CEO overconfidence has a positive effect on REM, and longer CAE tenure effectively reduces REM practices. However, CAE tenure did not moderate the relationship between CEO overconfidence and REM. This study contributed by emphasizing the importance of considering CEO personality traits and CAE tenure length in formulating effective corporate governance policies.

title: The Future of Finance: Recent Innovations and Strategic Shifts in Financial Management
summary: Abstract Financial management is an important exposure of a business. To establish and run a business there is a need of well knowledge of financial management. It includes supply of money, well profit, proper utilization of resources and creating safe investment chances. Innovations like FinTech, data driven decision making, AI in financial practices, increased Environmental, Social and Governance deposits, in addition organisations contributing to risk management, real time reporting, sustainability to maintain competitiveness in creating long lasting value. The article is related to Recent Innovations and Strategic Shifts in Financial Management. Important trends are AI, Machine and Advanced Analysis, Digital Transformation and Cloud-Based Systems, Sustainability, ESG and Ethical Investing, Open Banking, DeFi and Blockchain, Regulatory and Risk Management Pressures, Alternative Investments and Illiquid Assets. Article is purely theoretical and informative. the article is based on purely secondary data collected from various websites relating to financial management. Recent trends of financial management are moving towards increasing operational productivity but also delegates financial managers to play enhanced strategic role in organizational growth. Adoption of the recent trends are very essential for professionals to forward looking in economic landscape. It focuses on working capital, capital budgeting and revenue cycle.

title: Resource Dependence and Uneven Green Innovation Responses to Green Finance: Evidence from China’s Initial Pilot Cohort
summary: Green finance reforms may elicit different green invention responses across places with different inherited production structures. We examine the green finance reform and innovation pilot zones using a panel of 282 Chinese prefecture-level cities (2011–2024), with the main comparison drawn from the eight cities in the initial treatment cohort (three resource-based and five non-resource-based). Full-sample staggered-treatment estimators yield mixed diagnostics, motivating a common-timing difference-in-difference-in-differences design. The estimated resource–response differential is −0.657 log points (Webb wild-cluster p = 0.0049); the resource-city marginal response is imprecisely estimated rather than established as zero. The differential remains negative under province-by-year effects, alternative controls, and mapped-area exclusions, although saturated baseline-characteristic adjustments reduce its precision. Conventional and Webb pre-treatment tests disagree. An HonestDiD analysis shows that the confidence interval includes zero under modest departures from parallel trends, limiting a strong causal interpretation. Synthetic difference-in-differences fits pre-policy outcomes more closely in non-resource-based than resource-based cities. Pre-reform firm data indicate more concentrated brown-industry assets in resource-based cities but do not establish a mechanism. The results provide suggestive initial-cohort evidence of uneven responses to pilot designation, not direct evidence that green finance volumes or capability redeployment mediated the difference.

title: Key determinants of the growing importance of digitization and cybersecurity in economic processes and e-banking in recent years
summary: Objectives The article aims to identify and analyze key determinants of the growing importance of economic digitalization, e-banking, and cybersecurity. It also examines the relationships between ICT development, Industry 4.0, artificial intelligence, and the transformation of business models in enterprises and financial institutions. Material and methods The study employed critical literature analysis, comparative analysis of secondary data, and a systemic approach. Scientific publications, industry reports, and studies on digital transformation and cybersecurity were examined using an interdisciplinary perspective. Results The findings indicate that cloud technologies, mobile solutions, and AI systems are major drivers of digitalization and e-banking development. Accelerated digital transformation has strengthened e-commerce and electronic services while simultaneously increasing exposure to cyber threats and the need for advanced cybersecurity systems. Conclusions The growing role of digitalization and cybersecurity is structural and long-term in nature. The integration of technological innovations with comprehensive cyber risk management strategies is becoming essential for competitiveness, resilience, and sustainable development in the digital economy.

title: Corporate Social Responsibility in India: An Overview
summary: Abstract Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) has emerged as an important mechanism for promoting social welfare and sustainable development in India. This paper provides an overview of the statutory framework governing CSR under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013, including its applicability thresholds, expenditure requirements, committee structure, governance functions, reporting obligations, eligible activities under Schedule VII, and the treatment of unspent amounts. It also examines constitutional and ethical justifications for corporate responsibility, with particular reference to the right to life and a clean environment, the Polluter Pays Principle, and the relationship between business operations and stakeholder welfare. The paper highlights the role of CSR in supporting inclusive and sustainable development while noting the continuing importance of integrating environmental and social considerations into core business decisions.

title: Institutional Challenges and Digital Opportunities for Women Entrepreneurs
summary: Women Entrepreneurship is kind of a pillar that holds up global economic resilience, helps mix different kinds of jobs and somehow supports long-term social economic growth too. In today’s world Digital Transformation— driven by social commerce sites, cloud tools and new kinds of money tech— gives women founders fresh routes to get past older limits, mostly the ones that come from not having enough resources. Even so, there is still deep unfairness in the system. Biased ways of distributing funds, plus strict social rules keep slowing down the growth paths, and that part feels stubborn. This study builds a plan that looks at two sides, the help that comes from Digital Transformation, and the barriers that stay put. It zooms in on newer markets, for instance India. By using Institutional Theory and the 5Ms Framework, we can see how online shops, marketing efforts and FinTech money tools work like forces that lift Women Entrepreneurship. At the same time it checks why the digital gender gap stays around, why Capital Asymmetry keeps showing up in venture money decisions, and why work and home life clash for many women in daily reality. The study ends with evidence based policies that bring big economic players together with small businesses. The goal is to support the United Nations SDGs 5 and 8, and push Socio Economic Development so it can reach everyone.

title: The moderating influence of economic development on the effects of ESG, customer attitude and equity in banking: a comparative study of belt and road markets
summary: Purpose This study investigates the underexplored role of economic development in shaping customer interactions with environmental, social and governance (ESG) initiatives within banking services, using the consumer decision-making model. Design/methodology/approach This study compares customer attitudes, behaviors and equity related to ESG initiatives across belt and road markets: Hong Kong, Turkey and Africa (Kenya). Data from 817 participants (300 from Hong Kong, 245 from Turkey and 272 from Kenya) were analyzed using structural equation modeling. Findings The results show that ESG factors significantly influence customer attitudes and equity in full dataset in Turkey and Africa, while in Hong Kong, only governance factors matter. Customer attitude and equity in turn influence purchase intention in all regions. Crucially, the influence of ESG on customer perception is moderated by the level of economic development. Environmental concerns have a stronger impact in Africa and Turkey, with similar consumer responses in both countries. Governance initiatives have a stronger influence in Hong Kong. Customer attitude drives customer equity more strongly in Turkey and Africa. Practical implications These insights highlight the importance of considering economic development in ESG marketing strategies, helping marketers tailor their campaigns and enabling policymakers to develop effective ESG guidelines in diverse economic contexts across belt and road markets. This provides a better understanding of how economic development shapes ESG–consumer dynamics in banking. Originality/value The existing literature primarily focuses on how ESG factors influence firm value and overall economic progress. This is the first academic work that thoroughly explores how economic development influences the interaction between ESG and customers and is the first comprehensive cross-country on ESG-consumer interactions.

title: Impact of Digital Transformation on the Sustainability Performance of SMEs: The Moderating Role of Government Digital Support
summary: This study examines the association between digital transformation and the sustainable performance of small and medium-sized enterprises by considering the mediating roles of green innovation capability and dynamic capabilities and the moderating role of government digital support. The study integrates organizational capabilities and institutional support into a unified mechanism for explaining how digitalization is associated with economic, environmental, and social performance outcomes in an emerging economy. A two-stage design was employed: a qualitative instrument-refinement phase with structured discussions involving 35 enterprise directors in Ho Chi Minh City and Dong Nai, followed by a cross-sectional quantitative survey. This Study distributed 800 online questionnaires to respondents involved in digital transformation activities and retained 751 usable responses. The conceptual model comprised five reflective constructs and ten hypotheses. The study results show that digital transformation has the strongest direct positive association with sustainable performance and is also positively associated with green innovation capability and dynamic capabilities. Green innovation capability partially mediates the relationships between digital transformation and sustainable performance and between dynamic capabilities and sustainable performance. By contrast, dynamic capabilities do not independently mediate the digital transformation-sustainable performance relationship. Government digital support is positively associated with sustainable performance and strengthens the positive relationship between green innovation capability and sustainable performance. Given the cross-sectional, single-informant design, the findings are interpreted as associations rather than causal effects. The results suggest that managers should align digital investments with green innovation objectives, while policymakers should design digital support programs that help enterprises translate technology adoption into scalable, sustainable business outcomes.

title: Information Spillovers Across Media Markets: Risk Perceptions and Cyclospora Outbreaks in U.S. Bagged Salads
summary: From 2018 to 2022, contamination of fresh produce by Cyclospora cayetanensis, primarily affecting bagged salads, caused more than 3,300 outbreak-associated illnesses across the United States. Yet the economic consequences of these outbreaks, and the role of information exposure in shaping consumer responses, remain poorly understood. This study quantifies changes in bagged salad purchases and associated retail losses during six selected large multistate outbreaks occurring from 2018 to 2022 and examines how risk perceptions evolve across outbreak-affected and neighboring regions. Guided by a risk perception framework emphasizing risk proximity and information-driven belief updating, we integrate epidemiologic outbreak data, designated market area (DMA)-level Google Trends search intensity as a geographically granular proxy for information exposure, and NielsenIQ household purchase data. Because DMAs often cross state lines, this design identifies information spillovers to non-outbreak states sharing a media market. A Heckman selection framework accounts for purchase participation and unobserved heterogeneity, while complementary retail scanner data assess whether retailer stocking adjustments contributed to the observed purchase declines. Across the outbreak periods examined in this study, weekly bagged salad purchases declined by an average of 3.89%, implying cumulative retail losses of approximately $373.67 million. Outbreak-specific searches (e.g., "Cyclospora") were associated with greater perceived risk and larger purchase reductions, while general salad-related searches were associated with smaller reductions. Spillovers across shared media markets further reduced purchases in non-outbreak states by 3.33% per week. Retailer analysis found no statistically significant store-level stocking reductions during outbreak or recall periods, supporting the interpretation that the observed purchase declines were primarily demand-driven. These findings highlight the economic significance of information-driven consumer responses and the importance of timely, accurate, and geographically targeted risk communication during foodborne outbreaks.

title: A Literature Review on the Drivers of Corporate Carbon Performance Based on the Goal of Dual Carbon
summary: According to the Dual Carbon objectives, corporate carbon performance plays an important role in the low-carbon transition of China. The available reviews are largely reliant on literature published between 2010 and 2020 and do not offer enough information on the logic of the drivers in the new era; most of them just split the internal and external factors in general. This paper will choose core journals in both Chinese and English literature published between 2020 and 2026 and develop a three-dimensional analytical structure using external institutional policies, market stakeholders, and internal governance strategies using Chinese and foreign core literature in the same period. Carbon performance is defined as having two types, i.e., outcome-oriented and process - outcome integrated, and measurement criteria have not been made uniform. Internal digitalization, green innovation, and changes in managerial cognition may be the only methods of enhancing carbon performance due to external regulation and stakeholder pressure. The impact of different drivers is limited by the characteristics of the firm and the regional heterogeneity. The existing studies have such drawbacks as non-uniform measurement criteria and clusters of studies focused on listed companies. Based on these findings, the present paper suggests research opportunities that could be used as reference points for corporate decarbonization and policy enhancement.

title: Agricultural and Rural Big Data Policy and Agribusiness Supply Chain Resilience: Implications for Sustainable Agriculture in China
summary: Supply chain resilience supports sustainable agriculture by helping firms maintain operations and food supply during disruptions. This study examines whether agricultural digital public infrastructure strengthens agribusiness supply chain resilience, using China’s 2016 Agricultural and Rural Big Data Pilot Program as a quasi-natural experiment within a difference-in-differences design. The estimates indicate that the program significantly improves supply chain resilience. Exploratory channel analyses provide evidence consistent with bank-credit and corporate digital-transformation channels. The estimated gains are greater among state-owned enterprises, firms with digitally experienced executives, and firms in regions with higher internet penetration. Component analyses show positive estimates for agricultural data sharing, market-based investment and operational mechanisms, and big-data applications, whereas commodity-specific database development has no statistically detectable effect. These findings contribute to sustainability research by linking digital public infrastructure to the capacity of agribusinesses to withstand and recover from disruptions, an important foundation for the economic sustainability of agricultural supply chains. They also suggest that coordinated investment in data infrastructure, financing access, and digital capabilities may support more reliable agricultural supply and sustainable agricultural development, particularly in economies with fragmented production and limited information sharing.

title: Scaling Green Innovation Without Expanding the Bubble: How CSR Practices, Supply Chain Digitization, and Green Policies Shape Innovation Quality
summary: The rapid growth of green patent applications has raised concerns about a quantity–quality paradox in green innovation: rising patent application volumes do not necessarily translate into genuine technological progress or environmental value. Instead, they may create a green innovation bubble in which applications remain ungranted, consume organizational resources, and fail to generate technological value. While prior research has explored corporate social responsibility (CSR), digital transformation and environmental policies separately, few studies have incorporated them into a unified framework to investigate their joint impacts on green innovation. To address this gap, this study constructs an integrated analytical framework on three CSR dimensions (environmental investment, employee rest protection, and charitable donations) alongside supply chain digitization and institutional policy support. Drawing on stakeholder theory and the resource-based view. Using 11,288 firm-year observations from 1411 Chinese A-share-listed manufacturing firms during 2016–2023, we estimate two-way fixed-effects models and conduct robustness, propensity-score-matching, and heterogeneity analyses. Environmental investment and supply chain digitization increase green patent output but also widen the application–grant gap, whereas weak employee rest protection reduces innovation output and charitable donations are negatively associated with both outcomes. CSR interactions reveal conditional complementarity and resource competition. At the functional level, planning digitization raises output while reducing the imbalance, and production digitization also improves conversion quality. Ecological compensation and green finance jointly help redirect resources toward substantive innovation. The findings show that scaling green innovation requires coordinated environmental, human-capital, digital, and institutional resources rather than quantity-oriented expansion, providing an integrated sustainable environmental management pathway relevant to SDGs 8, 9, 12, and 13.

title: Enhancing Supply Chain Resilience Through Internet of Things Integration: A Systematic Literature Review
summary: This systematic review is based on a search of five bibliographic databases covering the period from 2019 to 2025, from which an explicit inclusion process selected 34 articles. The Internet of Things (IoT) enhances supply chain resilience by providing real-time operational visibility and, through its integration with artificial intelligence (AI), blockchain technology, and cloud computing, by reducing operational uncertainty. Several obstacles persist, such as limited interoperability, ineffective governance, and a skills gap, particularly in cybersecurity. Interest in supply chain research has grown in the literature over the past decade, but studies of resilience in emerging economies remain insufficient.

title: Corporate social responsibility in aviation management: The impact of sustainable marketing on brand equity
summary: This study seeks to investigate the impact of various aspects of corporate social responsibility (CSR) activities on sustainable marketing practices and brand equity in the aviation industry. The study used a quantitative approach, and data were collected from 490 employees working in the Turkish aviation industry using a well-structured questionnaire. The data were analyzed using the structural equation modeling (SEM) approach in the AMOS software package. Findings reveal that CSR practices targeting employees negatively affect strategic integration, while ethics-based practices positively influence strategic integration and ethical capabilities. CSR efforts aimed at society harm ethical capabilities but enhance social participation. Strategic integration and ethical capabilities positively affect brand equity components, whereas social participation has a negative impact. The findings suggest that the success of CSR efforts hinges on the strategic fit and ethical dimension of CSR rather than the social aspect of it alone. This research makes its contribution to the existing literature on CSR by expanding knowledge of the multidimensional links between CSR activities, sustainable marketing strategy, and brand equity in the aviation management setting.

title: The critical foundations of truly sustainable environmental auditing
summary: This essay addresses the urgent need for transformative action in environmental governance and examines how environmental auditing can support diagnostic and transformative agency within social-ecological systems. This requires a radical conceptual reconfiguration of environmental audit. To this end, the essay advances five conceptual foundations for a more impactful and sustainable approach. These include: an overarching commitment to Earth system stability; transcending an organization-centric paradigm; repositioning environmental auditing as a first-order function that drives, rather than follows, accounting; leveraging diverse forms of accounts to generate diagnostic insights into what truly matters within social-ecological systems; and actively coordinating accountability processes. Collectively, these foundations reposition environmental audit as a dynamic practice for nurturing meaningful change in social-ecological systems.

title: Does Financial Slack Matter? Corporate Governance, Corporate Activities, And Sustainability Reporting Quality in Indonesia
summary: This study examines the effects of corporate governance mechanisms and asset turnover on sustainability reporting quality, with particular emphasis on the moderating role of financial slack. Drawing on agency, legitimacy, and stakeholder theories, the study employs a quantitative approach using panel data from 33 companies consistently included in Indonesia's ESGQ-KEHATI Index between 2021 and 2024, yielding 132 firm-year observations. Sustainability reporting quality is assessed through content analysis of 33 environmental, social, and governance (ESG) indicators, while financial slack is measured as the ratio of free cash flow to total revenue. The data are analyzed using fixed-effects panel regression and moderated regression analysis. The findings reveal that the proportion of independent commissioners, audit committee, and total asset turnover positively and significantly influence sustainability reporting quality, whereas managerial ownership has no significant effect. Financial slack exhibits a positive direct association with reporting quality and strengthens the effects of independent commissioners and the audit committee, but does not significantly moderate the relationships involving managerial ownership or asset turnover. The adjusted R² increases from 0.514 to 0.533 following the inclusion of financial slack in the regression specification. Firm age is positively associated with reporting quality, while firm size has no significant effect. These findings suggest that financial flexibility complements formal corporate governance oversight in improving sustainability reporting quality. The study contributes to sustainability governance literature by demonstrating that the moderating role of financial slack differs across governance and operational mechanisms, highlighting the importance of resource availability in supporting effective sustainability oversight.

title: Unraveling supply chain resilience – performance relationships: insights from a smallholder agri-food chain
summary: Purpose This study examines the relationship between supply chain resilience and financial performance in smallholder agricultural supply chains. It seeks to explore the impact of different resilience elements on financial outcomes. Design/methodology/approach Data were collected by a survey of 276 supply chain actors in the lotus supply chain in Central Vietnam. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses were conducted to ensure the reliability and validity of the constructs, while structural equation modeling was employed to test the hypotheses. Findings The study revealed complex relations between resilience elements and financial performance in the smallholder agri-food chain. Among the elements, operational flexibility, readiness for disruptions, response agility and lower supply chain density were positively associated with financial performance. In contrast, efficiency, reserve capacity, financial strengths, recovery and supply chain criticality failed to demonstrate significant relationships in the smallholder agri-food chain context. Research limitations/implications Findings are based on one supply chain in Vietnam that might limit the generalizability. Originality/value The study expands resilience research to smallholder agricultural supply chains, highlighting the importance of certain resilience elements in volatile agri-food industries.

title: Social Media Influence on ESG Investment Intentions: Herding Effects Among Young Investors
summary: The rapid growth of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) investing has coincided with the increasing reliance of young investors on social media for financial decision-making. While digital platforms and financial influencers ("finfluencers") accelerate information dissemination, limited empirical work explains how digital cues interact with psychological biases in emerging markets. Drawing upon the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) and Social Influence Theory, this conceptual study proposes a framework to investigate the effect of social media exposure on ESG investment intentions among young retail investors in Malaysia, while examining herding behavior as a moderating mechanism. The proposed framework outlines a quantitative cross-sectional research design utilizing Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) to test the structural relationships. The paper provides theoretical insights into the convergence of digital media dynamics, psychological biases, and sustainable finance in emerging markets, offering practical implications for policymakers, financial institutions, and regulators.

title: Investigating the Health Benefits of Climate Finance: Evidence From Developing Countries
summary: ABSTRACT Although climate finance has expanded considerably over the past decades as part of the global response to climate change, many developing countries continue to experience persistently high infant mortality, widespread undernourishment, low life expectancy, and rising mortality burdens. This paradox raises an important question: does climate finance merely support environmental objectives, or does it also contribute meaningfully to improving population health in developing countries? Despite growing scholarly attention to climate finance, existing studies have largely focused on environmental sustainability, carbon emissions, and economic growth, while providing limited evidence on its broader health implications. To address this gap, this study examines the effect of climate finance on health outcomes in 61 developing countries over the period 2003–2021. Specifically, the study investigates the effect of climate finance on infant mortality, prevalence of undernourishment, life expectancy, and death rates. Employing the Driscoll–Kraay estimator and the Instrumental Variable Generalized Method of Moments techniques, the findings consistently reveal that climate finance significantly reduces infant mortality, undernourishment, and death rates while improving life expectancy. These results remain robust after controlling for endogeneity, omitted‐variable bias, alternative data structures, additional covariates, and disaggregated climate‐finance measures. Further evidence shows that both adaptation and mitigation finance contribute positively to population health. The study concludes that climate finance constitutes not only an environmental instrument but also an important mechanism for improving public health and human wellbeing in developing countries.

title: Mandatory vs Voluntary Corporate Social Responsibility: A Comparative Analysis of Corporate Social Responsibility Practices in India and Sri Lanka
summary: Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) has emerged as a vital aspect of modern corporate governance, emphasizing the accountability of businesses not only to shareholders but also to society at large. While CSR methods are extensively embraced worldwide, the regulatory approach to CSR varies greatly among countries. India has initiated a mandatory CSR framework under section 135 of the Companies Act of India (2013). This statutory obligation has created a structured approach compelling companies to actively contribute to social welfare, environmental sustainability and community development. In contrast, Sri Lanka continues to rely predominantly on voluntary CSR practices guided by soft law instruments such as the Corporate Governance Codes issued by the Colombo Stock Exchange and individual company policies. This study conducts a comparative analysis of the CSR frameworks in India and Sri Lanka focusing on the legal, regulatory and practical dimensions of mandatory versus voluntary CSR. This research examines how statutory obligations in India have influenced corporate behaviour and enhanced transparency and created measurable social impact while exploring the strengths and limitations of Sri Lanka’s voluntary CSR practices. The research identifies the gaps in Sri Lanka’s current CSR system, particularly in terms of enforcement, reporting standards and alignment with national development priorities. By analysing case studies, corporate reports and existing literature, this study aims to provide actionable insights and recommendations for Sri Lanka. It considers whether aspects of India’s mandatory CSR model can be adapted to strengthen Sri Lanka’s CSR framework, including potential statutory reforms, regulatory oversight and enhanced corporate accountability. This research contributes to the broader discourse on CSR by highlighting how legal mechanisms can shape corporate social engagement and societal outcomes. Ultimately, the study offers a policy-oriented perspective for enhancing CSR effectiveness in Sri Lanka.

title: Building Enterprise Supply Chain Resilience through Dynamic Capabilities: From Efficiency-First to Resilience-First
summary: The past five years of pandemic, geopolitical realignment and component shortages have exposed the structural fragility of efficiency-first supply chains and have raised supply chain resilience to the level of a strategic priority. The present study addresses that heterogeneity by re-reading the supply chain resilience literature through the dynamic capabilities lens. A structured narrative review was conducted, and fifteen representative studies were coded along the sensing, seizing and reconfiguring microfoundations and across six disruption types; reported standardised coefficients were extracted and synthesised descriptively. The results show that sensing research concentrates on multi-tier visibility, digital twins and predictive analytics, that seizing research centres on the redundancy-flexibility trade-off, and that reconfiguring research addresses regionalisation, reshoring and friend-shoring. The synthesised evidence indicates that seizing levers carry the largest reported effects on resilience and reconfiguring levers the smallest, and that conceptual coverage consistently exceeds empirical validation across all six themes examined. Research attention tracks the salience of recent events, leaving demand-side and financial disruptions under-examined. The study contributes an integrative capability map of a fragmented field and identifies the measurement of capability bundles as the principal research gap.

title: The Economic Effects of Digital Transformation on Chinese Listed Companies: An Investment Efficiency Perspective
summary: As China’s growth decelerates and its economic structure adjusts, the competitive advantages of traditional enterprises have eroded and corporate investment efficiency has declined. Understanding how corporate digital transformation transmits to the real economy is therefore the motivation for this study. Using Python-based text analysis, this paper constructs a corporate digital transformation index and, drawing on data from China’s A-share listed non-financial firms over the period 2012–2025, examines the impact of digital transformation on corporate investment efficiency. The analysis further explores the heterogeneous effects of digital transformation across firms differentiated by ownership structure, investment opportunities, and the intensity of external monitoring. The results show that higher levels of digital transformation alleviate financing constraints and reduce corporate governance costs, thereby enhancing investment efficiency. To address potential endogeneity concerns, a series of robustness checks are conducted, including instrumental-variable estimation, propensity score matching, the replacement of core variables and alternative estimation strategies, all of which yield results consistent with the baseline findings. Moreover, the positive effect of digital transformation on investment efficiency is particularly pronounced among firms with weaker external monitoring, non-state ownership, and more abundant investment opportunities.

title: Subsidy expiration and green innovation: does external financing have a role?
summary: Green innovation is a key driver for promoting the construction of ecological civilisation and achieving the carbon neutrality goal. This paper explores the relationship between subsidy expiration and green innovation. The findings are as follows: First, subsidy expiration inhibits green innovation by reducing R&D investment. Second, equity financing can alleviate the negative impact of subsidy expiration on green innovation. Third, enterprises do not invest the funds raised through equity financing into the R&D process, but instead increase the quantity of green innovation through strategic innovation, with investor attention playing a mediating role in this process. In addition, heterogeneous analysis reveals that the impact of equity financing on strategic innovation is more significant in non-state-owned and non-heavily polluting enterprises. This study provides practical guidance for enterprises to rationally utilise equity financing after subsidies expiration, and also offers important references for policymakers to optimise the subsidy withdrawal mechanism and accurately support enterprises’ green innovation.

title: Staged dual-network supply chain reconfiguration under escalating geopolitical disruptions
summary: We examine how global manufacturers reconfigure internal production networks and external supply chain relationships to sustain resilience and long-term viability amid escalating geopolitical disruption. Drawing on 42 semi-structured interviews with senior supply chain managers and industry experts across sectors and regions, we develop a process explanation of dual-network adaptation. Real options reasoning frames reconfiguration as a progression from reversible, option-preserving responses towards irreversible structural commitments. Institutional theory explains how geopolitical pressures constrain legitimate choices, while information processing theory illuminates how firms evaluate and coordinate them across networks. We find that disruption is experienced as an ongoing condition of corridor instability, regulatory reinterpretation, and growing legitimacy concerns rather than a single operational shock. Firms initially rely on rerouting, buffering, and multisourcing but undertake structural redesign when disruptions become persistent, recurrent, and correlated across alternatives, rather than merely severe. The findings explain how governance, coordination, and viability concerns shape staged dual-network reconfiguration.

title: Digital Technology-Enabled Configurations for Sustainable Supply Chain Resilience: A Dynamic QCA Study of Chinese Manufacturing Firms
summary: Supply chain resilience (SCR) has become increasingly important for maintaining stable and sustainable manufacturing operations under growing environmental uncertainty. However, existing studies mainly focus on the net effects of individual factors, providing limited understanding of how digitalization interacts with technological, organizational, and environmental conditions in shaping resilience over time. Drawing on the Technology–Organization–Environment (TOE) framework, this study examines how configurations of digitalization, research and development (R&D) investment, return on assets, asset turnover, and industry concentration are associated with supply chain resilience in Chinese manufacturing firms. Using a balanced panel of 300 firm-year observations from 60 Chinese listed manufacturing firms during 2019–2023, this study applies dynamic qualitative comparative analysis (DQCA) to identify multiple configurations associated with high and non-high supply chain resilience. The results show that no single antecedent condition is necessary for high resilience. Five configurations are identified for high SCR and five for non-high SCR, indicating equifinality and configurational asymmetry. The high-SCR solutions include both R&D-centered and digitalization-centered pathways, whereas low digitalization appears in four of the five non-high-SCR configurations. The relative coverage of these pathways changes across 2019–2023, with one digitalization-centered configuration (G2) becoming more prominent in the later years. These findings provide longitudinal configurational evidence on how different combinations of technological, organizational, and environmental conditions are associated with resilience over time.

title: Signaling Climate Transition Capacity: How Environmental Expenditures Attenuate the Carbon Risk Premium
summary: ABSTRACT This study investigates the pricing of carbon risk among publicly listed firms in Asia. We first develop a theoretical model of the carbon risk premium grounded in information asymmetry, which posits that a firm's environmental expenditures serve as a credible signal of its climate transition capacity. We then test these predictions using a novel panel dataset of 144 green bond issuers from 2005 to 2023. Our empirical analysis confirms the existence of a statistically significant, positive carbon risk premium in the region. Crucially, and consistent with our theoretical framework, we find that this premium is attenuated for firms with higher environmental expenditures. We further uncover that the modest scale of this premium is driven by investor heterogeneity: Long‐term institutional investors penalize high‐emitting firms but reward those with significant environmental spending, while short‐term strategic entities exhibit opposing behavior. Based on these findings, policymakers can mobilize corporate resources to address the carbon risk premium through three complementary levers: implementing stringent climate policy, enhancing climate finance taxonomies, and mandating standardized transition risk disclosure.

title: The Effects of Tax Planning, Financial Distress, and Earnings Management on Firm Value with Audit Quality as a Moderating Variable: A Study of Agricultural Subsector Companies Listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange During 2019–2024
summary: This study examines tax planning, financial distress, and earnings management in relation to firm value, with audit quality as a moderator. A balanced panel of 18 Indonesian listed agricultural firms provides 108 firm-year observations during 2019–2024. Fixed-effects estimates report positive predictor coefficients and negative audit interactions for tax planning and the distress proxy. The earnings-management interaction is not significant. Higher Altman Z-scores indicate better financial health. However, coefficient-test and model-fit statistics are inconsistent; inference remains provisional until checked against the original estimation records. The results do not establish causal effects.

title: Linking Sustainability Practices and Organizational Performance: A Systematic Literature Review and Thematic Analysis
summary: Background Sustainability practices are increasingly important for improving environmental responsibility, operational efficiency, competitiveness, and long-term organizational performance. However, research on Environmental Management Systems (EMS), Cleaner Production (CP), Green Innovation (GI), and Green Human Resource Management (GHRM) remains fragmented. This study systematically synthesizes these sustainability practices and their relationships with sustainable organizational performance while identifying major research gaps. Methods A systematic literature review and thematic analysis were conducted using studies retrieved from Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar following PRISMA principles. After identification, screening, and full-text assessment, 83 peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2015 and 2024 were included. The studies were analysed according to publication trends, geographical and industrial distribution, research methods, sustainability constructs, statistical techniques, mediating and moderating mechanisms, measurement approaches, and thematic patterns. Results EMS, CP, GI, and GHRM generally contributed positively to environmental, economic, and social dimensions of sustainable organizational performance, although some relationships were mixed or context dependent. GI showed the strongest concentration of positive findings. Research was predominantly concentrated in Asian countries and manufacturing industries and relied mainly on quantitative and cross-sectional designs. Seven major themes were identified, including environmental management capability, resource-efficient production, green innovation, employee-centred sustainability, performance measurement, contextual influences, and integrated sustainability implementation. Important mediators and moderators included green innovation, leadership, environmental strategy, stakeholder orientation, firm size, and competitive intensity. Conclusions Sustainability practices can enhance organizational performance, but their effectiveness depends on organizational and contextual conditions. The study integrates EMS, CP, GI, GHRM, and sustainable performance within a unified perspective and highlights the need for longitudinal, cross-country, service-sector, ESG-oriented, and digitally focused sustainability research.

title: Supply Chain Vulnerability in Health Systems: Management of Medical Supplies Import Dependency in Türkiye
summary: This study examines the evolution of Türkiye's dependence on imported medical products and its association with health supply vulnerability from 2002 to 2024. Guided by Resource Dependence Theory, a Health Supply Vulnerability Index (HSVI) was constructed from three dimensions: import dependency, exchange rate sensitivity, and financial pressure. Medical imports were converted from U.S. dollars to Turkish lira before the import-dependency ratio was calculated; public health expenditure and gross domestic product were expressed in compatible units; and all three indicators were transformed to a common 0-1 scale using Min-Max normalization. The normalized indicators were aggregated with equal weights, and robustness was examined using three alternative weighting schemes together with Pearson, Spearman, Kendall, absolute-deviation, and rank-stability measures. The HSVI reached its highest value in 2022 (0.640), followed by 2021 (0.612) and 2020 (0.551). These results identify periods of comparatively greater exposure to import dependence, exchange-rate movements, and fiscal pressure; they do not establish causal effects or directly measure product shortages. The findings also have policy implications, highlighting the need to strengthen domestic production capacity, establish strategic stock mechanisms for critical medical products, diversify suppliers, and develop adaptive supply management strategies to enhance the resilience and sustainability of Türkiye's health system during economic and global supply chain crises.

title: Debt Crowdfunding Growth and MSME Credit Risk in Indonesia’s Sustainable Digital Economy
summary: Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) in Indonesia often lack the collateral that banks require, and Peer-to-Peer (P2P) lending, the debt form of crowdfunding, has become a channel through which they raise capital in the digital economy. Lending now grows fastest outside Java, where platforms hold the shortest records on their borrowers. This study builds a monthly panel of 34 provinces from official statistics of the Financial Services Authority (Otoritas Jasa Keuangan/OJK) for December 2023 to December 2024 and estimates two-way fixed-effects models with standard errors clustered by province. The models test whether faster growth of outstanding loans is followed by a higher share of loans more than 90 days overdue (Tingkat Wanprestasi 90 Hari / TWP90) and whether this link differs between Java and the other regions. Outstanding loans rose by 29.1% to Rp 77.02 trillion, by 20.5% in Java and by 57.8% elsewhere, and MSMEs held 36.7% of the stock at the end of 2024. Current growth shows no significant link with TWP90. Growth three months earlier is followed by a lower TWP90 in Java, with a coefficient of −0.084 (p < 0.01), while outside Java the coefficient is only −0.011 (p = 0.079), and the gap between the two regions is significant (p < 0.01). Rapid P2P expansion was not associated with higher TWP90 during the study period, while the observed negative relationship between earlier loan growth and TWP90 in Java was substantially weaker outside Java. Platforms and regulators therefore need closer credit assessment where lending grows fastest if debt crowdfunding is to support MSME capital formation and the targets of Sustainable Development Goals 8 and 9. The evidence is associational and covers thirteen months, so longer panels with data specific to MSMEs are needed.

title: ETDP: a high-performance transportation delay prediction framework with explanations for supply chains
summary: Purpose This work aims to develop a transportation delay prediction framework to improve prediction performance while providing explanations for its predictions. Design/methodology/approach An ETDP (high-performance Transportation Delay Prediction Framework with Explanations) for supply chains is proposed, in which we design an LGFT (Local-Global Fusion Transformer) model for high-performance prediction, and integrate LGFT with SHAP to explain its predictions. LGFT captures local feature interaction patterns via 1D CNN and global nonlinear relationships via an MLP, which are then fused through a Transformer Encoder to model long-range contextual dependencies. Integrated with SHAP, ETDP formalizes a three-level explanation mechanism that can analyze global feature importance, key feature dependency, and instance-level attribution. Findings The ETDP framework is evaluated on three public supply chain datasets covering binary delay prediction, last-mile logistics, and five-class supply chain risk classification. On DataCo, ETDP achieves the highest precision and remains competitive across the other evaluation indicators. On India, it obtains the best recall, F1-score, and MCC in the held-out test evaluation. On Mendeley, it reaches the best accuracy, recall, MCC, and lowest FNR, while remaining descriptively close to XGBoost in F1-score, though below it in precision and probability-ranking metrics. Repeated-run analyses show statistically supported improvements over several representative baselines, although ETDP does not uniformly dominate every model and metric. Originality/value ETDP is a useful combination of predictive modeling and post hoc explainability for transportation delay prediction. Fusing local and global features, it contributes a high-performance prediction model. Integrating with SHAP, it provides a supply-chain-oriented three-level explanation workflow. It can support both early delay-risk sensing and more targeted intervention prioritization, such as strategic optimization, context-specific risk mitigation and specific order diagnostics. Source code is available at: https://github.com/Tang12333/Transportation-Delay-Prediction-Framework-ETDP

title: Sustainability reporting readability, stock liquidity and the role of corporate governance: evidence from an emerging market
summary: Purpose This study investigates whether the readability of sustainability reports affects stock liquidity and how corporate governance mechanisms shape this relationship. Drawing on agency theory, we ask whether investors reward clear non-financial disclosure. By answering this in Iran – a sanctioned emerging market with concentrated ownership – we test the boundaries of Western-developed theories and offer novel evidence from an institutionally distinct context. Design/methodology/approach Our sample comprises 612 firm-year observations from the Tehran Stock Exchange over 2016–2024. We measure sustainability report readability using the Gunning Fog Index and capture stock liquidity using three proxies: the bid-ask spread, Amihud’s illiquidity ratio and the average daily transactions. We examine four governance moderators: blockholder ownership, institutional ownership, board independence and audit firm type. The analysis employs panel data models with fixed effects and Newey–West adjustments. Findings More readable sustainability reports are associated with higher stock liquidity. However, this relationship depends on governance structures. Blockholder ownership and board independence significantly amplify the positive effect of readability on liquidity. Institutional ownership does not emerge as a significant moderator, and audit firm type matters only for specific liquidity measures. These findings suggest that governance mechanisms are not interchangeable; the institutional environment shapes their effectiveness. Originality/value This study offers one of the first empirical examinations of how corporate governance moderates the relationship between sustainability reporting readability and stock liquidity in an emerging market context. By locating the study in Iran – an economy shaped by prolonged sanctions – we provide a robust test of agency theory’s boundaries. The result is a refinement: some expected relationships hold, others do not, revealing how context conditions the financial consequences of disclosure transparency. These findings offer actionable insights for policymakers designing disclosure regulations and for investors and boards seeking to enhance market efficiency in institutionally challenging environments.

title: Stimulating the digital transformation of the construction industry in the Russian Federation
summary: The purpose of the study is to substantiate a system of economic and institutional instruments for stimulating the digital transformation of the Russian construction industry, taking into account the achieved level of information modelling adoption, regulatory changes and persistent digitalization constraints. The methodology combines system, comparative and structural-functional analysis, grouping and logical modelling. Official data and current Russian regulations are used. The study shows that mandatory information modelling requirements created a significant institutional impulse, while further adoption is constrained by high initial costs, skills shortages, uneven digital maturity, software interoperability problems and discontinuities of data acros lifecycle stages. The scientific novelty consists in a multi-level incentive mechanism that differentiates support by digital maturity and links public incentives to measurable operational outcomes.

title: Executive Technical Backgrounds, Strategic Attention, and Digital Transformation: Evidence from a Longitudinal Case Study of Haier Smart Home
summary: This paper investigates the strategic pathways for the digital transformation of manufacturing enterprises through a longitudinal case study of Haier Smart Home.Against the backdrop of rapid technological advancement and industrial upgrading, the study explores how the characteristics of the Top Management Team (TMT), particularly their technical backgrounds, appear to shape the direction and effectiveness of digital transformation strategies.Drawing upon Upper Echelons Theory and the attention-based perspective, the research examines the dynamic relationship between executive backgrounds, strategic attention allocation, and organizational transformation over 13 years.To achieve this objective, the study adopts a mixed-methods approach that combines TMT résumé analysis, text mining of annual reports, and financial indicator analysis.First, the study systematically analyzed senior executives'educational and professional backgrounds to identify how technical expertise evolved within the leadership structure.Second, annual reports spanning more than a decade were processed using text mining techniques to trace shifts in strategic attention toward digitalization, smart manufacturing, and innovation-related themes.Finally, financial performance indicators were examined to assess patterns in the economic outcomes that coincided with strategic transformation.The findings suggest that upper-echelon executive's technical orientation is associated with disclosed strategic emphasis.More importantly, shifts in strategic attention emerge as a potential explanatory pathway linking TMT characteristics to enterprise digital transformation strategies.The study further indicates that firms with technically oriented executives exhibit more pronounced digital transformation patterns and more marked movements in the financial indicators examined.Based on these findings, this paper proposes an evolutionary framework of "Executive Background -Strategic Attention -Strategic Transformation," suggesting the potential relevance of technical leadership in guiding manufacturing firms through digital transformation and offering practical implications for corporate governance and strategic management.As a single-case longitudinal study, these findings reflect observed patterns and exploratory inferences from one enterprise; interpret them with caution regarding generalizability to other firms, industries, or institutional contexts, and do not treat them as evidence of causal relationships.

title: Green Finance and Carbon Emission Intensity in South Africa’s Metal Production Sector: Evidence from an ARDL Approach
summary: This study investigates the impact of green finance on carbon emission intensity in South Africa’s metal production sector, utilizing the ARDL econometric model. South Africa faces the complex task of promoting economic expansion without compromising long-term environmental sustainability, given its fossil-fuel-dependent energy system and energy-intensive industries. Green finance, encompassing green credit, climate investment, and funding for eco-friendly projects, could be instrumental in mitigating emissions. This research analyzes both the short-term and long-term dynamics between green finance and carbon emission intensity, considering economic growth and metal output as additional explanatory variables. The findings indicate that green finance consistently reduces carbon emission intensity in both the long and short term. Over both horizons, annual gross domestic product growth was found to decrease carbon emission intensity, while metal production output was found to increase carbon emission intensity. These results offer valuable policy recommendations for achieving environmental objectives and long-term, responsible development. Overall, the findings deepen understanding of how financial systems can support climate mitigation efforts in emerging markets.

title: ESG Disclosure, Political Connections, and Financial Risk: The Moderating Role of Accounting Information Systems in Indonesian SOEs
summary: Background: Financial risk remains a critical governance concern for Indonesian state-owned enterprises (SOEs), particularly regarding sustainability disclosure, political connections, and accounting information systems (AIS). Objective: This study examines the effects of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) disclosure and political connections on financial risk and evaluates the moderating role of AIS. Methods: A quantitative explanatory approach was applied to 34 SOEs listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange during 2020–2024, comprising 170 firm-year observations. Secondary data were obtained from annual reports, sustainability reports, and financial statements. Financial risk was assessed using the Altman Z-score proxy, ESG disclosure through GRI indicators, political connections through board affiliation proportions, and AIS through ERP implementation. Data were analyzed using PLS-SEM with SmartPLS. Results: ESG disclosure had no significant effect on financial risk (β = 0.099; p = 0.234), whereas political connections showed a positive and significant association (β = 0.521; p < 0.001). AIS did not significantly moderate the ESG disclosure–financial risk relationship (β = 0.071; p = 0.280) or the political connections–financial risk relationship (β = −0.097; p = 0.296). Including moderation terms increased R² marginally from 0.260 to 0.275. Conclusion: Political connections are significantly associated with financial risk, whereas ESG disclosure and AIS moderation show no significant effects. These findings highlight the importance of strengthening SOE governance alongside accounting information system development.

title: Adaptive distribution strategies and supply chain performance in fragile economies with evidence from Coca Cola Mogadishu
summary: Supply chain management in fragile economies remains underexplored despite increasing operations by multinational firms in environments characterized by institutional instability, weak infrastructure, and security challenges. This study examines how outsourcing, distribution centers, and warehousing influence supply chain performance using evidence from Coca-Cola Mogadishu, Somalia. Drawing upon Agency Theory, Transaction Cost Economics (TCE), the Resource-Based View (RBV), and Institutional Theory, the study explains how firms adapt distribution strategies under conditions of institutional fragility. A quantitative cross-sectional design was employed using survey data collected from 144 employees across different managerial levels. The proposed model was analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings reveal that outsourcing and strategically managed distribution centers significantly enhance supply chain performance, whereas warehousing does not exert a significant effect in the study context. These results suggest that flexible coordination mechanisms and decentralized logistics capabilities provide greater resilience than asset-intensive infrastructure investments where governance systems and physical infrastructure are weak. The study extends supply chain literature by demonstrating that institutional fragility acts as an important boundary condition influencing the effectiveness of distribution strategies and explains why logistics capabilities that generate competitive advantage in stable economies may not produce similar outcomes in fragile states. The findings further provide practical guidance for firms operating in high-risk markets by highlighting the importance of outsourcing partnerships, strategically located distribution centers, and adaptive logistics configurations for improving operational resilience and supply chain performance.
