title: Corporate sustainability disclosure: systematic literature review of materiality, carbon, assurance, and ESG
summary: Corporate sustainability disclosure has become a major accountability instrument, yet prior studies in Indonesia remain fragmented by theme, sector, or company pair, and no integrated map of their development exists. This article systematically examined the development of research on the quality, materiality, and assurance of corporate sustainability disclosure. A qualitative systematic literature review was applied to twenty articles published in 2021–2026 and indexed in SINTA and other academic databases, and thematic content analysis grouped them by similarity of topics, methods, and research objects. Five themes emerged: conformity with the Global Reporting Initiative Standards, materiality assessment, carbon emissions and climate-related disclosure, assurance statement quality, and integrated environmental, social, and governance (ESG) practices with corporate governance. Disclosure quality among Indonesian companies was uneven across sectors and tended to be lower than that of multinational companies, and assurance practices were inconsistent because different standards, such as AA1000AS and ISAE3000, were used. Regulators and professional associations should issue more uniform assurance guidelines and apply double materiality more consistently, while companies should strengthen ESG committees and integrate sustainability risk management into governance to improve disclosure credibility.

title: Building Community and Supply Chain Resilience Against El Niño and La Niña Disruptions in Malaysia: Insights from a Qualitative Study
summary: Climate variability associated with El Niño and La Niña continues to generate significant challenges for communities, infrastructure, transportation systems, and economic activities in Malaysia. While previous research has focused primarily on environmental impacts, limited attention has been given to public experiences and their implications for resilience planning. This study investigates how Malaysians experience the impacts of El Niño and La Niña and identifies strategies that may strengthen community and supply chain resilience. A qualitative research design was adopted, and thematic analysis was performed on responses collected from 102 participants. Four key themes emerged: health and well-being impacts, disruption to daily activities and workplace operations, economic and resource-related pressures, and shared responsibility for climate adaptation. Participants described experiences of extreme heat, flooding, water shortages, transportation disruptions, and increased household expenses. Respondents also recommended improvements in drainage infrastructure, flood management, climate-risk communication, emergency preparedness, and environmental sustainability initiatives. The findings suggest that resilience to climate-related disruptions requires coordinated actions involving government agencies, communities, businesses, and individuals. This study contributes to the climate adaptation and supply chain resilience literature by providing empirical evidence of how Malaysians experience and respond to El Niño and La Niña disruptions, an area that has received limited attention in existing ENSO-related research. It further extends understanding of the link between community-level climate experiences and broader supply chain resilience planning within the Malaysian context The study further highlights the importance of proactive planning to minimise disruptions to infrastructure, transportation systems, organisational operations, and supply chain activities. These findings offer practical implications for policymakers, infrastructure planners, and supply chain managers seeking to improve climate resilience in Malaysia.

title: The Study of Digital Transformation, Artificial Intelligence and Their Implications for Future Research
summary: Digital transformation changes the conditions under which organizations produce and use knowledge. Artificial intelligence adds new ways to search, predict, generate, and evaluate information. Yet greater use of these tools does not establish that research becomes more reliable or more original. This paper develops a critical narrative review and descriptive secondary-data analysis to examine that distinction. Selected publications on organizational change, AI-assisted work, scientific discovery, and governance provide the conceptual foundation. Published statistics from Stanford's AI Index and Eurostat illustrate changes in adoption between 2023 and 2025. The two series are analysed separately because their populations and measurement procedures differ. The evidence indicates expanding use, but adoption statistics cannot demonstrate causal improvements in research quality. An original conceptual framework links digital foundations and AI capabilities with changes in research practice, conditioned by human expertise, institutional arrangements, and governance. Four propositions translate the framework into questions for future testing. The proposed agenda prioritizes reproducibility, task-specific evaluation, skill development, equitable participation, and preservation of intellectual diversity. The paper concludes that future research should evaluate the complete knowledge-production process, including verification and correction costs, rather than treating faster output as sufficient evidence of progress. No primary survey, experiment, or model validation is claimed. The contribution is an integrated account of how organizations can study AI-enabled transformation while maintaining the evidentiary standards needed for credible knowledge

title: DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION AND SERVICE DELIVERY IN THE NIGERIAN TELECOMMUNICATIONS INDUSTRY
summary: This study examined the effect of digital transformation on service delivery in the Nigerian telecommunications industry. An ex-post facto design was adopted, using annual secondary data from 2001 to 2024 (24 observations) sourced from the Nigerian Communications Commission, the Central Bank of Nigeria and the National Bureau of Statistics. Service delivery was proxied by a composite Service Delivery Quality Score, which averaged 0.1714. Digital transformation was captured by mobile phone penetration, internet penetration, mobile money transaction and telecommunication network coverage, with literacy rate as a control. Unit root tests revealed a mixture of I(0) and I(1) series. The Autoregressive Distributed Lag bounds test confirmed cointegration (F = 4.8293), exceeding the 1% upper bound of 4.15. Long-run estimates showed that mobile phone penetration (β = 0.1598, p = 0.0171), telecommunication network coverage (β = 0.0119, p = 0.0000) and literacy rate (β = 0.0591, p = 0.0082) significantly improved service delivery. Internet penetration (β = −0.0503, p = 0.2750) and mobile money transaction (β = −0.1473, p = 0.2782) were negative and insignificant. The error correction term (−0.6007, p = 0.0000) indicated that about 60.07% of disequilibrium is corrected annually, and the short-run model explained 89.58% of the variation in service delivery. Diagnostic tests confirmed normal residuals, no serial correlation, homoskedasticity and parameter stability. The study concluded that infrastructural reach, rather than usage intensity, sustains service quality. It recommended prioritised investment in network coverage, deeper mobile access and targeted digital literacy programmes.

title: Financial Management and Economic Sustainability in Sociobiodiversity Supply Chains: Evidence from Family Farming in the Brazilian Cerrado
summary: The research examined financial management as a strategic factor associated with the economic sustainability of family farming production units engaged in sociobiodiversity supply chains, with a focus on the municipality of Iporá, Goiás, Brazil. It was based on the understanding that the sociobiodiversity products of the Brazilian Cerrado, in addition to their environmental, social, and cultural value, can be an important source of income and help strengthen rural communities when supported by appropriate management practices. From this perspective, the research sought to understand how family farmers in the region organize their financial management processes, establish pricing strategies, control production costs, and use management tools. It also aimed to identify the main challenges and opportunities related to the economic sustainability of these activities. Furthermore, a practical guide was developed to assist producers in addressing real challenges encountered throughout the production process. Methodologically, the research was characterized as exploratory and descriptive, adopting a mixed-methods approach that drew on a literature review, documentary analysis, field observations, and questionnaires administered to 52 family farmers, selected through non-probabilistic convenience sampling, in the region, and analyzed through descriptive statistics and Fisher’s exact test. The findings indicate that, although sociobiodiversity represents a relevant alternative for generating employment and income, significant weaknesses remain in the financial management of production units, particularly regarding the informality of financial controls (only 15.4% use spreadsheets and 57.7% do not separate household from production expenses), difficulties in measuring production costs (only 25.0% calculate them in detail), and limited access to financial resources. These findings are specific to the studied region and should not be generalized beyond this context.

title: Do ESG Bonds Signal Lower Climate Transition Risk Exposure? Evidence from the Korean Market
summary: This study examines whether the first-time issuance of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) bonds by Korean listed firms is priced by the stock market as a signal of reduced climate transition risk.Using a sample of 46 first-time ESG bond issuers from 2019 to 2021, including 44 firms with sufficient return histories for the main CAR analysis, alongside firm-level measures of climate risk exposure, this study finds no evidence that investors interpret issuance as a positive climate risk signal.Stock returns around issuance dates are, if anything, negative rather than positive, and are statistically insignificant in the main event window under the cross-sectional-correlation adjustment used here.This study does not detect statistically significant heterogeneity between highcarbon and other issuers; the negative point estimates are more pronounced among nonfinancial issuers.Although firms' climate risk exposure appears lower after issuance in simple before-after comparisons, the decline largely precedes issuance and the matched difference-in-differences estimates for climate risk exposure are statistically insignificant.The findings have the following limitations: the effective samples are small (44 firms for the main CAR analysis and 20 matched pairs in the supplementary DiD analysis) and clustered in 2021; the issuance date provides a less precise event date than an announcement date; and the matched design has limited common support.The findings indicate an absence of detectable effects rather than evidence of no effect, and no causal interpretation is drawn.The pattern is consistent with ESG bond issuance in the Korean market reflecting issuer selection and financing needs rather than a credible climate risk signal, an interpretation that is not directly tested here.

title: Pre-registration: four tests for a non-Chinese rare earth supply chain (Lynas, Iluka, MP Materials), with dated forward predictions

It also states the scoring rules and the baseline figures read from company reports on 28 October 2026. ## Question, cases and window Which tests of viability has each case passed between July 2025 and June 2026, and which has it not? Cases: Lynas Rare Earths (Australia, with separation in Malaysia), Iluka Resources (Eneabba refinery) and MP Materials (United States, comparator). The subject is the three companies, not a country. Quantitative window: 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026 (Lynas fiscal year 2026). Events after the window are reported only as dated events, up to 31 October 2026. ## Four tests and scoring rules (denominators declared by the companies) - P1, light oxides: NdPr produced in the window divided by the nominal capacity target declared by the company (Lynas: 12,000 t per year, FY25 results, 28 Aug 2025). At least 90 %: pass; 50 to 90 %: pass with conditions; below 50 %: fail. - P2, commercial viability without state support: share of new capacity or revenue that depends on a public price floor or public financing. Above 50 %: no evidence of viability without support; 10 % or less: pass; in between: pass with conditions. - P3, heavy rare earths: Dy+Tb produced divided by the nominal target of the new heavy-separation plant (300 t per year, Lynas announcement of 29 Oct 2025, plant not yet built). At least 50 %: pass; 10 to 50 %: pass with conditions; below 10 %: fail at scale. - P4, downstream: magnet product sold by allied plants linked to the case. Lynas Dy+Tb production in the September 2026 quarter is 30 t or less. It fails if it exceeds 30 t. - F3. MP Materials reports price-floor income above US$10 million in Q3 2026. title: Communicating for Resilience: Risk Communication and Community-Based Disaster Preparedness through The Corporate Social Responsibility Program of Pt Pertamina Patra Niaga Fuel Terminal Poso
summary: Disaster preparedness requires not only access to risk information but also effective communication, community participation, and multi-stakeholder collaboration. This study aims to analyze risk communication practices in the Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) program Disaster Response School implemented by PT Pertamina Patra Niaga Fuel Terminal Poso in Moengko Village, Poso Regency, Central Sulawesi. The study employs a qualitative descriptive approach, with data obtained through in-depth interviews with six informants representing the company, village government, Disaster Preparedness Team, disaster management agency, school, and community, as well as program documentation. The results indicate that risk communication is conducted through face-to-face awareness sessions, visual media, interactive training, and evacuation simulations. This approach provides participants with the opportunity to understand safety procedures and practice basic preparedness skills. Community involvement in determining evacuation routes and safety needs also highlights the importance of two-way communication that bridges technical knowledge with local experience. Collaboration among the company, government, school, and community supports program implementation, while the local philosophy of Sintuwu Maroso, which emphasizes unity and togetherness, serves as a relevant cultural context for collective preparedness. However, several challenges remain, including equitable participation, training continuity, coordination of information updates, and the maintenance of safety facilities and institutional capacity as CSR support is reduced or comes to an end. This study underscores the importance of sustainable, participatory, and risk communication adapted to the local context in supporting community-based disaster preparedness. The findings primarily represent the experiences and perceptions of the informants, rather than a measurement of long-term impacts on behavioral change or disaster risk reduction.

title: Understanding adaptation to digital transformation: evidence from Indian advertising industry
summary: Introduction Digital Transformation (DT) is changing the advertising industry by influencing how professionals design their campaign strategies, cooperate with clients, collaborate with teams, and develop new skills in response to technological and market demands. While the existing literature has primarily focused on consumers and advertising platforms, it has given limited attention to the lived experience of advertising professionals as they adapt to and navigate DT. This study fills this gap by exploring how Indian advertising practitioners comprehend and interpret organizational adaptation to DT. Method The present research employed a qualitative approach, using in-depth semi-structured interviews with 40 advertising professionals selected through purposive sampling across different roles. Data were analyzed using inductive thematic analysis conducted through ATLAS.ti to develop themes explaining how advertising practitioners experience DT. Result The analysis revealed four themes: disruption forces, tensions within the industry, adaptation, and transformation of advertising work. Together, they conceptualize DT as a dynamic and interconnected process rather than a series of isolated changes. The findings revealed tensions centered on technological complexity, extensive consumer data, budget limitations, changing consumer behavior, threats from emerging digital agencies, and a lack of digital talent. In response, professionals are adopting digital tools, embracing flexible work practices, and reorganizing their agency structure to stay agile and competitive. However, as working practices continue to evolve in a digital environment, they generate new tensions that require further adaptation. Discussion A Recursive Tension—Adaptation Framework, a conceptual model, is proposed based on an analysis of Indian Advertising Professionals’ experiences, explaining how professionals within advertising organizations continuously adapt to an evolving digital work environment and offering implications for managing organizational change and workforce development.

title: Spatial spillover effects of the digital economy on green innovation based on time varying networks
summary: Introduction The digital economy reshapes interregional connections beyond geographical proximity, with implications for green technology innovation. Methods Using 2014–2023 panel data for 30 Chinese provinces, this study constructs an asymmetric, time-varying digital-economic network based on a modified gravity model and applies social network analysis and a Spatial Durbin Model. Results The results show that the network exhibits a persistent core–periphery structure alongside changes in provincial positions. Under the baseline network specification, digital economy development is positively associated with local green technology innovation and has a significant negative indirect effect on network-connected provinces, consistent with resource-competition and siphon-related forces outweighing knowledge-diffusion forces in the cross-regional channel. This negative indirect effect remains significant under an alternative geographic matrix, although the negative total effect becomes insignificant, indicating that the overall effect is sensitive to the definition of spatial linkages. Conditional decomposition shows that the negative spillover deepened before 2019, moderated between 2019 and 2021, and remained stable thereafter. Discussion Provincial evidence suggests that stronger connectivity does not necessarily improve the relative innovation performance of late-developing regions, as its benefits depend on local absorptive capacity and resource-retention capabilities. These findings highlight the importance of combining interregional digital connectivity with local innovation-capacity building.

title: Strategic digital transformation from digital value creation to business sustainability in SMEs
summary: Purpose Digital transformation presents substantial opportunities for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) but also necessitates strategic changes. Motivated by value creation, it involves delivering digital offerings through innovative business models. From a resource-based view (RBV), digital transformation creates competitive advantage. However, realizing this potential requires strategies that combine digital technologies with business objectives. Design/methodology/approach This empirical analysis is based on data from 203 Finnish SMEs. The study examines the connection between digital value creation, via digital collaboration and digital channels, and business sustainability, positing that relationships can be mediated through digital strategy measurements. Findings Digital value creation alone does not necessarily lead to positive sustainability outcomes for SMEs. Creating value in digital settings is more complex; however, when combined with digital strategy measurements, its positive effects on the social, environmental, and economic dimensions of sustainability are conveyed. Research limitations/implications The results identify digital strategy measurement as a key capability mediating digital value creation and business sustainability in SMEs. By adopting a RBV lens, this study advances the understanding of the digital transformation–sustainability nexus. Practical implications SMEs should integrate digital value-creation activities into a comprehensive digital strategy and guide them through measurements. Grounding digital strategies in sustainability principles and using effective measurement enables evaluation, implementation, and organizational learning, enhancing strategic success. Originality/value This study shows that digital value creation is insufficient for improving business sustainability in SMEs and establishes digital strategy measurement as essential for conveying its benefits, supporting the pursuit of more sustainable business models.

title: Adaptive Environmental Governance and Local Community Resilience in Addressing Tidal Flood Risks in the Peat-Coastal Lowlands of Indragiri Hilir Regency
summary: Tidal flooding in Indragiri Hilir Regency, Indonesia, is expanding amid lowland geographical conditions and environmental degradation, while disaster management remains reactive and community adaptation is insufficiently integrated into environmental governance. This study examines the ecological and anthropogenic drivers of tidal flooding, environmental policies, disaster budgeting, and community adaptation strategies to inform sustainable coastal environmental policy. A qualitative explanatory-critical case study was conducted in Indragiri Hilir Regency, Riau Province. Data were collected through semi-structured in-depth interviews, field observations, and document analysis and analyzed through data condensation, thematic categorization, data display, and conclusion drawing and verification. The findings indicate that the number of subdistricts affected by tidal flooding increased from three in 2019 to six in 2021. Identified drivers included land conversion in water infiltration areas, mangrove degradation, riverbank settlements, and sedimentation and waste accumulation in canals. Environmental governance was constrained by the absence of specific regulations and the Regional Disaster Management Agency’s (BPBD) annual budget of IDR 1 billion for managing multiple disaster types. Community adaptation strategies included maintaining seed reserves, adjusting planting calendars, undertaking independent evacuations, and collectively cleaning canals. These findings highlight the importance of integrating local adaptation strategies into environmental governance. The study recommends strengthening regulations, adopting risk-based budgeting, rehabilitating ecosystems, and enhancing government–community collaboration to support a transition from reactive disaster management toward sustainable coastal environmental governance.

title: The connection between digital transformation and the innovation potential of Chinese commercial organizations of various ownership types
summary: Subject. Features of the digital transformation process in China, its impact on the economic performance of state-owned and private enterprises. Objectives. An empirical evaluation of the nature and strength of the relationship between digital transformation and the innovation potential of Chinese companies. Methods. Mathematical analysis tools were applied. Results. State-owned enterprises are characterized by a higher intensity of scientific research, but digital tools partly replace traditional forms of research activities. For private companies, such a substitution effect has not been observed. Conclusions. The form of ownership acts as an important institutional moderator of innovation activity. The results obtained can be taken into account when developing differentiated digitalization strategies, considering the institutional characteristics of enterprises.

title: What Do ESG Scores Reflect? Disclosure, Risk, and Institutional Ownership in Korean Listed Firms
summary: 본 연구는 2015~2024년 유가증권시장 상장기업의 KCGS, 서스틴베스트, S&P Global, Bloomberg ESG 점수를 연도별 백분위 순위 점수로 변환하여, 해당 점수가 공시, 논란, 소유구조 중 무엇을 반영하는지 검토한다. 분석 결과는 다음과 같다. 첫째, KCGS 기반 공시 지수는 ESG 점수를 설명하지만, 이 결과는 공시 지표의 선택에 의존한다. 둘째, ESG 점수와 차년도 ESG 논란 발생 간의 음(-)의 관계는 발견되지 않는다. 즉, ESG 점수의 리스크 식별 기능이 확인되지 않는다. 셋째, 외국인지분율과 ESG 점수의 양(+)의 관계는 유의하며, 공시 수준에 의한 부분 매개 패턴에 부합한다. 반면 기관투자자지분율에서는 이러한 패턴이 확인되지 않는다. 넷째, 그린워싱 가설은 지지 되지 않았다. 다만 논란 표본의 검정력에 한계가 있다. 이상의 결과는 ESG 점수가 위험 신호로 기능하지 못하며 공시 수준에 상당 부분 의존함을 시사한다.

title: Digital Transformation and Operational Efficiency in Banking Under Regulatory Solvency Requirements
summary: Background Digital transformation can be linked to banking efficiency through the reorganization of processes, the expansion of digital services, and investment in technology; however, this link may vary depending on each institution’s institutional capabilities and regulatory and operational conditions. Method A quantitative, non-experimental, longitudinal approach was adopted. Documentary data from three Peruvian banks were organized into a balanced panel of 33 bank-year observations. Indices of digital transformation and operational efficiency were constructed, and descriptive analyses and linear regressions were performed, incorporating bank effects and time trends. The variables were standardized, and inferences were evaluated using HC3y standard errors and, additionally, Driscoll-Kraay standard errors. Results The average digital transformation index rose from 33.17 points in 2015 to 78.39 in 2025, while operational efficiency showed a fluctuating trend. The overall digital transformation index showed a positive but not significant association with operational efficiency (β = 0.439; 95% CI: −0.415 to 1.294; p HC3 = 0.302; p DK = 0.265). Process automation, service digitization, and technology investment also recorded positive coefficients, although these were not significant. Nor was there sufficient evidence of moderation by regulatory solvency or geographic coverage, as the low or negative values of the adjusted R 2 indicated limited explanatory power. Conclusion The expansion of digital transformation was not accompanied by a uniform and statistically verifiable improvement in operational efficiency. The findings should be interpreted as exploratory relationships specific to the banks and the period analyzed, without attributing causal associations or generalizing them to the financial system as a whole.

title: Climate Protest and Firm ESG Performance: Elucidating Global North–South Inequalities
summary: ABSTRACT In response to calls to keep global warming below 1.5°C, firms have employed responsible business practices in their operations. Neglecting their normative and ontological ethical obligations to their stakeholders has often attracted climate protests, posing a potential risk to business operations and their reputation by threatening their social licence. This study examines how climate protests influence corporate environmental management performance, highlighting disparities among firms in the Global North (GN) and Global South (GS). We use panel regression with fixed effects to analyse data on 3485 large firms worldwide between 2020 and 2024, comprising climate protest data from the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace and Environment, Social and Governance (ESG) performance data obtained from the London Stock Exchange Group. Our study finds that climate protests are positively and significantly associated with firms' environmental performance. Protest size also correlates positively, though to a lesser extent. Notably, protests in the GN exert a stronger influence and impact than those in the GS. Additionally, a firm's human rights record positively predicts its environmental performance, highlighting the interconnectedness of corporate social and environmental responsibility. The results further reveal significant variation across firms, with the association between climate protests and environmental performance being most pronounced among firms with lower ESG ratings. Our findings underscore the need for firms and investors to integrate the potential of climate activism into their environmental risk management strategies and highlight regional disparities in corporate climate responsiveness.

title: From Information Sharing to Knowledge Flow: Digital Transformation as a Moderator of Communication Strategies in Kenya’s Public Benefit Organizations
summary: Purpose: Kenya’s Public Benefit Organizations (PBOs) run on information. They must account to donors and regulators, coordinate programmes spread across counties, and hold on to what they learn when staff and funding move on. Many struggle to do so: in 2024/2025, more than 4,779 PBOs faced deregistration for non-compliance, and only 61% of active organizations filed annual returns. This study examined whether communication strategies and digital transformation, treated as channels through which organizational information and knowledge flow, explain PBO performance. Methodology: The study was anchored on Dynamic Capabilities Theory, with the knowledge-based view of the firm as a supporting lens. A pragmatic, mixed-methods cross-sectional survey targeted a stratified random sample of 368 of the 4,750 PBOs registered and compliant with PBORA, with one respondent per PBO, and 261 returned usable questionnaires (70.9%). Ordinal logistic regression, including a moderation model with an interaction term, was applied to the quantitative data, and open-ended questionnaire responses were analysed thematically. Findings: On their own, communication strategies did not have a significant influence on performance (β = −0.046, p = .818). Respondents explained why. Channels were fragmented, feedback loops were weak and staff resisted new practices, so information moved without becoming shared knowledge. Digital transformation told a different story. It had a significant positive influence on performance (β = 0.495, p = .017) and strengthened the link between communication and performance (interaction β = 0.111, p = .036), working as the infrastructure that captures, circulates and preserves what organizations know. Implications to Theory, Practice and Policy: PBO leaders need to treat communication as a knowledge process, backed by digital feedback channels, shared repositories and data-driven reporting. For regulators, the priorities are digital reporting standards, sound data governance and digital skills across the sector. Few studies have examined nonprofit communication and digital transformation in Africa through an information and knowledge management lens. This one does, and its evidence points to a simple but consequential conclusion: communication is associated with performance mainly when it is digitally enabled and built into how the organization works.

title: Nonlinear coupling between digital economy development and regional income inequality in a reproducible multi-agent simulation framework
summary: As a core driver of global economic growth, the digital economy reshapes regional economic landscapes and income‑distribution patterns. Existing work mostly estimates linear or single‑threshold relationships under static‑equilibrium assumptions, limiting the understanding of feedback between technology diffusion, capital reallocation and regional heterogeneity. This work adopts multi‑agent simulation to build an “economic‑geographical” dual‑gradient coupling model for interacting heterogeneous enterprises, residents and governmental agents on a spatial lattice. Simulations rely on a fully documented synthetic benchmark generated with fixed seed (1642026), without observational statistical, survey or satellite data; parameters are configured rather than econometrically calibrated. Therefore, outputs provide a reproducible simulation framework and mechanistic hypotheses rather than empirical estimates. Simulation results show that inequality variation is primarily explained by the technology‑diffusion gradient (52.8–66.4%), followed by capital‑flow (25.3–31.8%) and institutional gradients (8.3–16.4%). The technology‑capital contribution gap narrows from 41.1 pp in the Pearl River Delta to 22.0 pp in the Northwest at lower development levels. The DEI‑Theil link is monotonic with no interior turning point; thresholds 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8 are predefined model inputs, and the relationship disappears after first‑differencing (coefficient = 0.060, p = 0.262). Digital‑infrastructure investment stands out as the single policy tool reducing western inequality by 15.2% by 2040, while 0.5–50 km lattice‑resolution tests generate deviations below 0.054%. Owing to the synthetic benchmark, these results have no external validity.

title: DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION IN SHARED SPACES: BUILDING THE SÃO JOSÉ COWORKING WEB PLATFORM
summary: This study aimed to develop and implement a full-stack web platform to support the digital presence and service communication of São José Coworking, located in São José dos Pinhais, Paraná, Brazil. The research adopted an applied case study approach, combining a literature review, an analysis of organizational requirements, platform development, and a preliminary assessment of its implementation and usage. The technological architecture integrated HTML, CSS, and JavaScript in the front-end, PHP in the back-end, and MySQL for data storage. The resulting platform was deployed to the organization's official domain, providing information about its facilities, services, plans, and contact channels. Website usage was examined using Google Analytics data collected between September 24 and October 21, 2026. During this period, the platform recorded 233 active users, including 227 new users, approximately 1,300 events, and an average engagement time of 22 seconds per active user. The results provide preliminary evidence of platform access and interaction, particularly with service and contact pages. However, the available data do not establish improvements in administrative efficiency, customer acquisition, or organizational competitiveness. The study demonstrates the practical application of full-stack technologies in a shared workspace and provides a foundation for future evaluations of usability and organizational impact.

title: Corporate Fraud and Regulatory Mechanisms in India
summary: Corporate fraud is a serious threat to the integrity of markets, the protection of investors, and public confidence in business institutions. It may involve the deliberate falsification of accounts, diversion of assets, bribery, market manipulation, concealment of liabilities, related-party abuse, or misleading disclosures. In India, the problem is addressed through a combination of company law, securities regulation, financial-sector supervision, criminal investigation, audit regulation and corporate-governance requirements. The framework includes the Companies Act, 2013; the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992; listing and disclosure regulations; banking laws; and the work of institutions such as the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, Serious Fraud Investigation Office, Securities and Exchange Board of India, Reserve Bank of India, National Financial Reporting Authority and enforcement agencies. This paper examines the principal forms and causes of corporate fraud, the legal and institutional mechanisms used to prevent and investigate it, and the continuing challenges in enforcement. The Satyam Computer Services scandal and the Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services crisis are considered as examples of how weak oversight, misleading financial information, governance failures and delayed detection can damage stakeholders. The paper argues that India has developed a substantial formal framework, but effective protection depends on implementation: timely information sharing, competent investigation, independent boards and auditors, credible whistle-blower systems, proportionate sanctions, and stronger financial literacy. It concludes that regulation should combine deterrence with early detection and organisational cultures that reward truthful reporting.

title: STRATEGIC DEVELOPMENT OF TOURISM IN UZBEKISTAN THROUGH FORESIGHT TECHNOLOGIES IN THE CONTEXT OF DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION
summary: The article examines the strategic development of tourism in Uzbekistan through foresight technologies in the context of digital transformation. It discusses how digital platforms, data analytics, artificial intelligence, scenario planning and stakeholder engagement can support evidence-informed tourism policy. Based on a theoretical analysis of policy documents and international research, the article proposes an integrated framework linking digital readiness, foresight methods, destination management and sustainable development. A phased implementation model is presented, including horizon scanning, scenario development, pilot initiatives and continuous monitoring. The article argues that foresight should not be treated as a precise prediction of the future; rather, it is a structured process for exploring alternative futures and preparing flexible strategic responses. The proposed approach may help public authorities, tourism businesses and local communities improve resilience, visitor experience and the long-term competitiveness of Uzbekistan's tourism sector.

title: FIRM SIZE, BOARD CHARACTERISTICS AND ESG PERFORMANCE: EVIDENCE FROM INDONESIA
summary: Growing pressure for corporate sustainability highlights the critical need to understand how governance structures drive corporate environmental, social, and governance (ESG) practices. Utilizing data from 38 Indonesian listed firms between 2020 and 2024, this research analyzed how firm size mediates the impact of board characteristics (size, independence, and gender diversity) on ESG performance. A total of 190 firm-year observations sourced from Refinitiv were analyzed using the Structural Equation Modeling–Partial Least Squares (SEM-PLS) approach. The results indicated that larger and more independent boards positively influenced firm size, whereas board gender diversity unexpectedly exhibited a negative effect. Crucially, firm size significantly drove ESG performance and acted as a vital mediating mechanism across all board characteristics. These robust results demonstrated that the impact of board governance on sustainability outcomes was heavily channeled through organizational scale, providing critical perspectives for policymakers and managers in emerging markets.

title: DATA AS A FINANCIAL ASSET: HOW FINTECH COMPANIES USE CONSUMER BEHAVIOUR DATA FOR PERSONALISATION, RETENTION, AND REVENUE GROWTH
summary: This study examines how FinTech companies transform consumer behaviour data into financial value through artificial intelligence, predictive analytics, and hyper - personalisation. It explores how transactional, behavioural, and demographic data are collected, analysed,and converted into personalised financial products, recommendations, interfaces, and communication strategies. The study further evaluates how these practices influence customer retention, customer lifetime value, return on investment, average revenue per user, customer acquisition cost, and churn. Particular attention is given to machine learning, customer segmentation, recommendation systems, and predictive models used to anticipate consumer needs and improve engagement. The paper also considers the strategic role of data in product development, cross-selling, and marketing optimization. Alongside these benefits, it critically examines privacy, consent, algorithmic bias, cybersecurity, and regulatory compliance. The study concludes that AI-driven personalisation can create substantial commercial value in FinTech, but sustainable growth depends on transparent, secure, fair, and responsible use of consumer data over the long term.

title: Revisiting sustainability performance: a review of definitions, conceptualizations, theoretical perspectives, and future research agenda
summary: This study systematically reviews and synthesizes contemporary scholarship on sustainability performance (SP) to clarify its conceptual foundations, dimensions, and theoretical underpinnings across multiple sectors. The review aimed to examine how sustainability performance has been defined, operationalized, and applied, while identifying key research themes and emerging directions with implications for health and sanitation projects. Using established systematic literature review (SLR) protocols, 302 peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2020 and 2025 were analyzed. Studies were categorized by conceptualization, sectoral focus, theoretical orientation, and methodological design. The findings reveal that SP is predominantly framed through the Triple Bottom Line (economic, environmental, social) and Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) frameworks, with increasing integration of Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) indicators. The most represented sectors include corporate management, manufacturing, construction, agriculture, energy, and tourism, while healthcare and sanitation remain significantly underexplored. Commonly applied theories include Stakeholder Theory, Institutional Theory, Legitimacy Theory, Resource-Based View, Dynamic Capabilities, and Sustainability Transitions Theory. Thematic synthesis identifies four dominant research clusters: measurement frameworks, sectoral applications, drivers and barriers, and links to resilience and long-term competitiveness. Overall, the review integrates fragmented perspectives, advances conceptual clarity, and proposes a future research agenda emphasizing context-sensitive, socially responsive, and project-based sustainability, particularly within public health and sanitation systems that underpin community resilience and inclusive development.

title: ESG Funds Research: A Bibliometric and Thematic Analysis of Emerging Trends
summary: Environmental, social, and governance (ESG) funds have received increasing research attention in recent years, yet the extant literature appears fragmented, with few attempts to bring together the scholarly works and chart out intellectual progression and future research themes. This systematic review article attempts to fill this gap by providing a comprehensive overview of ESG fund research with respect to its evolution, intellectual roots, and emerging trends. A total of 322 publications indexed in Scopus were identified, of which 67 studies were eligible following PRISMA-informed screening via Bibliometrix (R). Citation analysis, co-citation analysis, bibliographic coupling, and thematic analysis were conducted to map out prolific authors, journals, countries, knowledge clusters, gaps, and future directions. Results show that research on ESG funds has progressed from initial discussions around ethics and corporate social responsibility (CSR) toward recent interest in sustainable finance, data-driven decision-making, investment performance considerations, and regulatory developments. The studies primarily draw upon literature from CSR, finance, and environmental sustainability. The United States, China, and India account for most of the publications, while African, South American, and Eastern European countries are rarely represented. ESG, mutual funds, and sustainability form the prevailing themes of interest, while machine learning, Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation, greenwashing, and resilience through crises are identified as potential future directions. This article reviews the literature on ESG funds using PRISMA-guided bibliometric mapping techniques. The review synthesizes the literature on ESG funds found in finance, sustainability, business ethics, and accounting. It maps the field’s knowledge base, conceptual foundations, thematic trends, and future research avenues, and provides an integrated framework for future research on ESG funds.

title: Digital Transformation and Management Capability in National Defense Posture: The Moderating Role of Defense Industry Self-Reliance
summary: Digital transformation has become central to defense modernization, yet evidence remains limited on how digital capabilities and management capacity interact with national defense-industry self-reliance to shape national defense posture. This study examines the direct effects of digital transformation, management capability, and defense-industry self-reliance, and tests whether self-reliance changes the effects of digital transformation and management capability on defense posture. The conceptual model integrates Dynamic Capability Theory, which explains organizational sensing, seizing, and transformation processes, with the Resource-Based View, which emphasizes strategic resource endowments. A cross-sectional survey produced 225 usable responses from personnel and officials associated with Indonesian defense institutions. The constructs were measured with 90 perception-based items and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling with bootstrapping and predictive assessment. Digital transformation had the strongest positive direct effect on national defense posture, followed by management capability and defense-industry self-reliance. Defense-industry self-reliance significantly weakened the positive relationship between digital transformation and defense posture, contrary to the predicted direction, while it strengthened the relationship between management capability and defense posture. The model explained 75.4 percent of the variance in national defense posture and showed substantial out-of-sample predictive relevance. The negative moderation indicates that industrial localization can create short-term compatibility, resource-allocation, certification, and implementation frictions when domestic capabilities are not synchronized with digital modernization. The study contributes by showing that strategic resources do not automatically amplify dynamic capabilities; their value depends on alignment and implementation timing. Policy should therefore prioritize interoperable digital architectures, phased localization, technology-transfer milestones, and managerial capability development so that industrial self-reliance complements rather than constrains digital defense transformation.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Digital Transformation in Higher Education: A Systematic Review of Opportunities, Challenges and Emerging Trends
summary: Artificial Intelligence AI is getting more and more involved in higher education, it is reshaping teaching, learning , assessment, academic administration, research, and even how institutions decide things. In the last few years the fast rise of generative artificial intelligence GenAI, plus intelligent tutoring systems, learning analytics, automated assessment, recommendation systems, and AI assisted administrative tools has opened up new possibilities for universities, yet it also brings worries like academic integrity, data privacy, algorithmic bias, digital inequality, transparency, and changing professional roles. This paper actually uses a secondary-data based systematic review, looking at research and policy sources about AI and digital transformation in higher education. The review brings together outcomes from academic studies, other systematic reviews, and international policy frameworks, sort of to map out the main uses, opportunities, obstacles, and the kind of emerging trends that are starting to show up. What the literature suggests is that AI in education is not only about making content. It also includes adaptive learning, personalized tutoring, intelligent assessment, profiling and prediction, and support for institutional management. At the same time, good adoption does not just happen, it needs institutional policies, AI literacy, ethical safety nets, teacher professional development, careful responsible assessment approaches, and a human centered way of putting things into practice. A number of recent international frameworks stress human agency, ethics, AI competencies, and responsible usage, so there is a clear direction there. Overall the review shows that AI is best understood as augmentation tech with AI to help educators and learners not to flip a switch and replace the educational roles that already exist. For digital transformation a balance must exist, with technical novelty on one side and pedagogical sense together with ethical norms institutional realities and human factors, on the other. None of those should be treated as optional because leaving one out tends to break the system quickly.

title: Correlated Demand Shocks and Asset Pricing
summary: Abstract I propose a mechanism through which institutional investors’ correlated demand shocks provide a source of market risk in asset pricing. Institutional investors have mandates to beat a similar market index. During periods of strong stock market performance, their incentive to outperform intensifies as more of them fall short of the market index. This incentive induces procyclical risk-taking behavior, generating correlated demand that elevates the market betas and risk premia of exposed stocks. Quasi-experiments using exogenous changes in index membership support a causal interpretation of the mechanism. Elevated betas are associated with a higher perceived cost of capital and reduced firm investment. (JEL G1, G2)

title: Effect of Corporate Environmental Disclosure on Investor Decisions in the Oil and Gas Sector in Nigeria
summary: Backgrounds: Corporate environmental disclosure is increasingly important to investors, yet Nigerian studies examine it only in aggregate, obscuring which specific dimensions drive investor response. Objectives: This study specifically assesses the effects of environmental policies and practices disclosure, environmental expenditures and investments disclosure, GHG emissions disclosure, compliance with environmental regulations disclosure, and environmental audits and certifications disclosure on market capitalization. Methodology: The study adopted a quantitative correlational research design using secondary panel data drawn from the annual reports, sustainability reports, and financial statements of all 13 oil and gas companies, covering the five-year period 2019 to 2023 (65 firm-year observations). A binary content-analysis disclosure checklist was used to construct an index score for each disclosure dimension, and data were analysed using descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, and panel regression. Findings: Environmental policies and practices disclosure (β = .34, p < .001), GHG emissions disclosure (β = .29, p < .01), and environmental audits and certifications disclosure (β = .31, p < .001) each had significant positive effects on market capitalization, while environmental expenditures and investments disclosure (β = .18, p < .05) and compliance with environmental regulations disclosure (β = .21, p < .01) also showed significant, comparatively smaller positive effects. Conclusions: Corporate environmental disclosure across all five dimensions is significantly and positively associated with market capitalization, with policy disclosure and third-party audit certification exerting the strongest effects. Firms should strengthen policy communication and pursue independent audits and certifications, while regulators should standardize disclosure requirements.

title: Corporate Governance Failures and Fraud Investigation: A Comparative Study of India's Serious Fraud Investigation Office and International Corporate Fraud Investigation Agencies
summary: Corporate fraud in India has repeatedly exposed the weakness of the governance structures meant to prevent it, as the Satyam and IL&FS collapses show. India’s institutional answer is the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO), which has wide investigative and coercive powers under the Companies Act, 2013 but depends on the Central Government for the decision to prosecute. This study asks whether that dependence, rather than any shortage of investigative power, is the SFIO’s central institutional weakness. The study is doctrinal and comparative. It traces the SFIO’s origin in the recommendations of the Naresh Chandra Committee, analyses its statutory framework and arrest powers, and compares it with the UK Serious Fraud Office, the US Securities and Exchange Commission and Department of Justice, and Australia’s ASIC. It then surveys the Indian case law testing the SFIO’s powers and formulates a five-element institutional effectiveness framework covering investigative independence, coercive powers, prosecutorial integration, resource capacity and accountability. The study finds that the SFIO’s powers are broadly comparable to those of its international counterparts, that most litigation concerns the procedure of its actions rather than the substance of its findings, and that its clear weakness lies in prosecutorial integration. It recommends, among other reforms, an independent civil enforcement track for the SFIO modelled on the Australian experience.

title: Producing spatial justice: Scalar governance and territorial differentiation in coastal China’s nuclear development
summary: Nuclear infrastructure development highlights an important empirical case in environmental governance: nuclear facilities concentrate environmental and social burdens locally, yet many projects proceed without sustained opposition. In the context of China, this paper argues that such outcomes are produced through county-level scalar governance strategies. Focusing on the Zhangzhou Nuclear Power Project, the study reconstructs how local authorities designed four concentric governance zones (20 km, 10 km, 2 km, 200 m) and calibrated distance-based interventions—compensation and relocation, tiered emergency planning and monitoring, graded communication and participation, and differentiated infrastructure and welfare investments—so that governance intensity corresponded to spatial exposure. Drawing on archival materials, policy documents, and semi-structured interviews with officials and project actors, corroborated by administrative records and implementation milestones, the analysis shows that scalar governance pursued distributive, procedural, and recognition objectives across zones. Importantly, the absence of organized resistance is interpreted not as conflict resolution but as the managed incorporation of grievances into institutional channels within a constrained political environment. By reframing nuclear legitimacy as the outcome of territorially differentiated state action, the paper contributes to debates on territory, scale, and environmental governance and positioning spatial justice as a conditional mechanism for managing uneven infrastructural risk.

title: Mapping the architecture of innovation capacity in MENA: a systemic fuzzy DANP analysis of interdependent drivers and causal pathways
summary: Purpose This study aims to model the complex causal architecture and network interdependencies of national innovation capacity in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region, moving beyond linear composite indices to identify key leverage points and systemic dynamics. Design/methodology/approach Using a Fuzzy Decision-Making Trial and Evaluation Laboratory-based Analytic Network Process (Fuzzy DANP) methodology, the authors analyze 25 indicators across five dimensions: human capital, institutional framework, knowledge creation, green innovation and market sophistication. As a proof of concept, they use a literature-informed influence matrix and a synthetic data set, constructed from realistic parameter ranges for 20 MENA economies, to enable the analysis of causal weights, net effects and influence networks. The model’s structural logic is benchmarked against the Global Innovation Index (GII). Findings The results illustratively reveal green innovation as the most influential dimension, followed by institutional framework and human capital. The analysis identifies regulatory quality, R&D expenditure and environmental taxes as pivotal net-cause variables. The causal mapping shows institutional framework and human capital as foundational drivers, while the network analysis visualizes a strong institutional-knowledge core and positions green innovation as a systemic integrator. Research limitations/implications While the use of a literature-informed influence matrix and synthetic data establishes a proof-of-concept, future research should populate the model with empirical data and formal expert judgments (e.g. Delphi panels) for country-specific diagnostics. Practical implications The findings provide clear, stakeholder-specific guidance. Policymakers should prioritize strengthening foundational institutions and mission-oriented green innovation policies. Industry and academia must collaborate to transform human capital into an innovation conduit. The results further highlight a strategic opportunity for Islamic finance to fund green and technology ventures through instruments like Mudarabah and green sukuk. Social implications This study underscores that targeted, systemic innovation policy is critical for addressing the MENA region’s core challenges of sustainable diversification, youth employment and climate vulnerability. Originality/value This study makes a novel methodological and conceptual contribution by applying fuzzy DANP to map the MENA innovation system as a complex adaptive network in a synthetic/illustrative framework. The study further integrates region-specific institutional and financial characteristics, including Islamic finance mechanisms, conceptually into the systemic analysis of innovation capacity.

title: DO ESG AND BOARD STRUCTURE IMPROVE FINANCIAL PERFORMANCE? EVIDENCE FROM INDONESIAN FAMILY FIRMS
summary: The consideration of socioemotional wealth in Indonesian family firms might create tension between sustainability and economic objectives. This study aims at examining how environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance and board structure affect the financial performance of Indonesian family firms. Drawing on the resource-based view and socioemotional wealth perspective, ESG is conceptualised as a strategic capability, and board structure represents a governance mechanism that shapes its effectiveness. Panel data were used from family firms listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange between 2011 and 2023, with firm and year fixed effects; the results showed that both ESG performance and board structure positively influence profitability. Moreover, the positive effect of ESG is stronger in firms with smaller boards, suggesting that more cohesive governance enhances the implementation of ESG strategies and their financial benefits. Ultimately, these findings highlight the importance of governance in enabling family firms to realise greater value from ESG, particularly in emerging markets.

title: Capability-building before transformation: How manufacturing SMEs pursue Industry 4.0 through operational-first digital transformation
summary: Digital transformation has become critical for manufacturing competitiveness, yet small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) often struggle to leverage Industry 4.0 technologies because of limited resources and underdeveloped capabilities. While prior research highlights the role of dynamic capabilities and organisational ambidexterity in digital transformation, less is known about how SMEs themselves diagnose digitalisation challenges and prioritise improvement initiatives. This study analyses 17 Detailed Development Plans prepared by manufacturing SMEs within a national Industry 4.0 readiness programme. Using the Gioia methodology, we examine nearly 900 pages of self-assessed challenges and proposed actions. The results suggest that SMEs predominantly interpret Industry 4.0 adoption through an operational lens, emphasising real-time data capture, shop-floor control, and process stabilisation rather than strategic innovation or business model renewal. However, selected cases indicate early planned elements of organisational ambidexterity, where exploitation-oriented digitalisation is combined with exploratory initiatives such as R&D activity, modular capability expansion, and new production technologies. For managers, the findings suggest linking operational digitalisation roadmaps to small-scale exploratory experiments that may help firms gradually move toward ambidextrous capability development. For policymakers, the results indicate that support instruments should follow graduated, capability-staged transformation pathways rather than assuming SMEs are ready for advanced digital adoption.

title: When do book–tax differences matter for earnings persistence? The role of sales decline
summary: This study examines the association between book-tax differences (BTDs), sales decline, and earnings persistence among non-financial listed firms in Vietnam. Adopting a conditional perspective, the study treats BTDs as observable signals of accounting-tax divergence, reporting environments, and transitory earnings components, while sales decline is conceptualized as an adverse operating state that may weaken the association between current and future earnings. Using a balanced panel of 325 firms from 2013 to 2023, comprising 3,575 firm-year observations, earnings persistence is measured through the association between current and one-year-ahead pre-tax book income. Earnings are further decomposed into operating cash flows and accruals to examine component-level persistence. The empirical analysis uses OLS regressions with industry and year fixed effects and firm-clustered standard errors. Additional analyses control for earnings management and tax avoidance and test the robustness of the findings using a continuous measure of sales decline, a sample excluding the COVID-19 period, and an alternative annual-decile classification of large BTDs. The results show that pre-tax book income is persistent, but its persistence is significantly lower during periods of sales decline. The evidence for BTDs is asymmetric: large positive BTDs are more consistently associated with lower earnings persistence, whereas the evidence for large negative BTDs varies across model specifications and earnings components. The three-way interactions among sales decline, BTD classifications, and current earnings are not statistically significant in the main analyses, indicating that the evidence does not support a broad BTD-specific amplification mechanism. Overall, the findings suggest that earnings persistence is shaped by earnings components, accounting-tax reporting signals, and operating conditions. The study highlights the importance of interpreting BTDs jointly with sales trends and earnings components in the Vietnamese institutional setting.

title: Pengaruh Literasi Keuangan Syariah dan Financial Technology terhadap Inklusi Keuangan pada Mahasiswa Ekonomi Syariah Universitas Pamulang
summary: Inklusi keuangan syariah nasional masih jauh di bawah inklusi keuangan keseluruhan, dan bukti dari mahasiswa program studi ekonomi syariah masih terbatas. Penelitian ini menguji hubungan literasi keuangan syariah dan financial technology (fintech) dengan inklusi keuangan, serta menilai batas interpretasi hasil ketika indikator fintech dan inklusi keuangan berdekatan secara konseptual. Penelitian memakai pendekatan kuantitatif asosiatif dengan desain potong lintang. Sampel berjumlah 100 dari 529 mahasiswa Program Studi Ekonomi Syariah Universitas Pamulang, dipilih dengan purposive sampling berdasarkan kriteria yang telah ditetapkan sesuai dengan tujuan penelitian. Data dikumpulkan melalui kuesioner skala Likert lima poin (22 butir) dan dianalisis dengan regresi linear berganda menggunakan SPSS 26. Literasi keuangan syariah (B = 0,387; t = [6.528]; p < 0,001) dan fintech (B = 0,356; t = 6.018; p < 0,001) berhubungan positif dan signifikan dengan inklusi keuangan. Model menjelaskan 84,1% variasi skor inklusi keuangan pada sampel ini (R² = 0,841; F = 255,897; p < 0,001). Hasil tersebut menunjukkan asosiasi statistik pada sampel dan tidak menetapkan hubungan sebab akibat. Kontribusi penelitian berupa bukti empiris dari satu program studi ekonomi syariah dan pembahasan kritis tentang tumpang tindih indikator fintech dan inklusi keuangan yang perlu diuji pada penelitian berikutnya.

title: Green Finance and Economic Growth: A Literature Review
summary: Green finance has emerged as a critical catalyst for driving economic innovation and facilitating the global transition toward carbon neutrality and sustainable economic development (Marín‐Rodríguez et al., 2024; Yadav & Chandiok, 2025). This literature review provides a systematic bibliometric analysis and qualitative meta-synthesis of scholarly work published between 2013 and 2023, following PRISMA 2020 guidelines to examine the causal links between green financial instruments to environmental and macroeconomic performance (Çıtak & Hoş, 2024; Olugbenga & Bali, 2026). The study categorizes existing research into three primary dimensions: the mechanism of green capital allocation, the efficacy of regulatory policy frameworks, and the differentiated regional impacts of financial innovation (Liu et al., 2025; Ma & Chen, 2025). Key findings highlight that while green credit and bonds effectively redirect capital toward climate-aligned projects, their success is heavily moderated by institutional quality and regulatory clarity (Ali et al., 2025). Furthermore, the integration of emerging technologies—such as artificial intelligence and block chain—is identified as a vital driver for enhancing transparency, risk assessment, and operational scalability within climate-finance ecosystems (Bagarti & Pahwa, 2025; Singh et al., 2025). Despite these advancements, significant barriers remain, including fragmented policy regulations, high transaction costs in emerging markets, and a persistent “instrument-impact paradox” caused by the lack of standardized environmental accounting metrics (Jamali & Voghouei, 2025; Raman et al., 2025). The review concludes that achieving a resilient global green finance architecture requires a shift toward interdisciplinary research, unified global reporting standards, and the active role of development banks in de-risking sustainable investments (Liu et al., 2025; Sheraz et al., 2021). Ultimately, these findings offer a policy-action roadmap to align financial incentives with long-term ecological sustainability and the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (Majumdar et al., 2026; Olugbenga & Bali, 2026).

title: Modeling ESG Performance Drivers in the Shipping Industry: An LLM‐Assisted q‐ ROFRS‐Delphi‐WINGS‐FCM Framework for Causal Analysis and Simulation
summary: ABSTRACT The shipping industry plays a vital role in global trade and also exerts significant environmental and social pressures due to high fuel consumption, greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, and intensive port activities. Implementing environmental, social, and governance (ESG) practices offers a strategic pathway to enhance sustainability performance in this sector; however, it remains difficult to determine which managerial and operational actions can most effectively drive improvements in ESG performance. To address this challenge, this study proposes a novel framework that integrates a large language model (LLM), an extended q‐ rung orthopair fuzzy rough set ( q‐ ROFRS)‐based Delphi‐weighted influence nonlinear gauge system (WINGS) model, and a fuzzy cognitive mapping (FCM) simulation. This approach systematically identifies critical success factors (CSFs), analyzes their cause–effect relationships, and simulates their dynamic influence on ESG performance in the shipping industry. The findings reveal that six CSFs, including structured board oversight, global policy engagement, comprehensive legal compliance framework, employee‐centric culture, effective communication strategy, and integrated water resource management, serve as key causal drivers within the ESG system. FCM‐based scenario simulations suggest that full activation of these modeled drivers could substantially improve projected ESG performance under the assumed scenario conditions. This research offers a dual contribution: Theoretically, it extends fuzzy decision‐making and AI‐driven causal modeling to complex sustainability systems; practically, it provides actionable guidance for shipping companies and policymakers to strengthen ESG integration, meet the International Maritime Organization's net‐zero targets, and advance the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

title: DETERMINAN PENGELOLAAN KEUANGAN GENERASI Z DI DESA TUNGGARA, BANJARNEGARA
summary: Sound financial management is an essential competence for Generation Z, who grow up in a digital environment with heavy exposure to consumption trends. This study examines the effects of financial literacy, hedonistic lifestyle, self-control, Fear of Missing Out (FoMO), and financial technology (fintech) on the financial management of Generation Z in Tunggara Village, Banjarnegara Regency. A quantitative survey design was used. Primary data were collected through a Likert-scale questionnaire distributed via Google Forms to 100 respondents aged 16–29 years, selected by purposive sampling from a population of 479, and analyzed with multiple linear regression. Financial literacy (B = 0.591; p < 0.001), self-control (B = 0.165; p < 0.001), and fintech (B = 0.142; p = 0.010) have positive and significant effects on financial management, whereas hedonistic lifestyle (p = 0.614) and FoMO (p = 0.675) have no significant effect. The model is feasible (F = 57.954; p < 0.001) and explains 75.5% of the variance in financial management. Financial literacy is the most dominant determinant (standardized beta = 0.561). The findings highlight the need for applied financial education, stronger self-control, and prudent fintech use among rural Generation Z.

title: The Impact of Digital Transformation on Human Resources Management: A field study on public and private sector organizations in the city of Jeddah, 2024-2025
summary: على الرغم من تنامي الاهتمام البحثي بالتحول الرقمي، تظل الدراسات الكمية التي تفحص أثر أبعاده المتكاملة على كفاءة إدارة الموارد البشرية في البيئة السعودية محدودة. تهدف هذه الدراسة إلى قياس أثر أبعاد التحول الرقمي على كفاءة إدارة الموارد البشرية في منظمات القطاعين الحكومي وشبه الحكومي والخاص بمدينة جدة، في ظل محدودية الدراسات الميدانية التي تناولت هذه العلاقة في البيئة السعودية بصورة شاملة. واعتمدت الدراسة المنهج الوصفي التحليلي، وطُورت استبانة وفق مقياس ليكرت الخماسي، وطُبقت إلكترونياً على عينة قصدية بلغت (40) مفردة من العاملين في القطاعات المستهدفة. وأظهرت نتائج اختبار الثبات أن معاملات كرونباخ ألفا تراوحت بين (0.877–0.915) لأبعاد الدراسة، وبلغت (0.965) للأداة ككل، كما تأكد صدق البناء باستخدام معاملات ارتباط بيرسون، مما يعكس ارتفاع مستوى الاتساق الداخلي للأداة. وأظهرت النتائج ارتفاع مستوى توافر أبعاد التحول الرقمي بصورة عامة، حيث جاءت البنية التحتية التقنية في المرتبة الأولى، بينما جاءت المهارات والقدرات الرقمية في المرتبة الأخيرة بدرجة متوسطة. كما سجل بُعد الرضا الوظيفي والتعلم المستمر أعلى متوسطات أبعاد إدارة الموارد البشرية، تلاه بُعد كفاءة إدارة الموارد البشرية. وأكدت نتائج تحليل الانحدار المتعدد وجود أثر ذي دلالة إحصائية لجميع أبعاد التحول الرقمي على إدارة الموارد البشرية، حيث مثّلت القيادة التحويلية والثقافة التنظيمية أقوى المتغيرات تفسيراً للتباين، تلتها المهارات والقدرات الرقمية، ثم البنية التحتية التقنية، وأخيراً الاستراتيجية والحوكمة الرقمية، مع تفسير النماذج نسبة مقدارها R²=0.456 من التباين في المتغير التابع، وبلغت قيمة F(4,35)=7.341 عند مستوى دلالة إحصائية (p<0.001).
