title: When Financial Reporting Readability Matters for Audit Effort: The Role of Conditional Conservatism
summary: This study examines whether conditional conservatism attenuates the additional audit effort associated with low financial reporting readability. Using 11,167 firm-year observations for 859 US non-financial firms listed on the New York Stock Exchange from 2010 to 2022, we estimate panel regressions with year and industry fixed effects. Readability is measured with five linguistic indices, audit effort is proxied by audit fees and audit delay, and conditional conservatism is captured through a firm-year asymmetric timeliness measure. Higher readability is associated with lower audit fees and shorter audit delays. More importantly, the positive interaction between readability and conditional conservatism indicates that these negative associations weaken as conditional conservatism increases. Drawing on agency and signalling theories, we interpret conservatism as an accounting-based mechanism that constrains optimistic reporting and enhances perceived reporting credibility. The study connects textual disclosure quality with accounting recognition practices and shows that auditors’ responses to narrative complexity depend partly on the properties of the underlying accounting numbers.

title: Green Human Resource Management: Past, Present, and Future Trends
summary: The growing importance of sustainability has transformed organizational approaches, and Green Human Resource Management (GHRM) is emerging as a pivotal driver to achieve environmental, social, and competitive objectives. This present study conducts a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of GHRM research articles published during 2005-2025, based on Scopus and Web of Science datasets. A total of 4,462 unique articles were analyzed to examine publication trends, dominant research themes, influential papers, and collaboration patterns among countries and institutions. The present study employed RStudio and Bibliometrix as instruments for conducting the bibliometric analysis of the extracted data. Findings reveal a steep rise in GHRM-related research after 2018, with China being the largest contributor, followed by the USA, India, Pakistan, and Malaysia. The key research themes that have been identified are GHRM, green innovation, and environmental performance. Directions for future research emphasize technological advances and cross-regional collaboration.

title: Top management attributes and market valuation across economic regimes: an ESG accountability signalling perspective from an emerging EU capital market
summary: Purpose This study examines whether the market-valuation associations attached to female and foreign executive representation, managerial interlocks and managerial ownership differ between stable and crisis periods, and whether the observed patterns are compatible with an Environmental, Social, and Corporate Governance (ESG) accountability-signalling perspective alongside competing governance interpretations. Design/methodology/approach The study uses Orbis data for non-financial Warsaw Stock Exchange firms over 2017–2023. Baseline difference and system Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) estimates are supplemented by CRE/Mundlak and firm fixed-effects specifications. The governance variables are based on the available 2023 records, and treated as structurally persistent; main coefficients therefore rely primarily on cross-sectional differences between firms, while COVID interactions capture regime-contingent valuation differences. Findings In the baseline system GMM, female and foreign executive representation and managerial interlocks are positively associated with firm valuation during stable periods. Their COVID-period interactions are negative; combined COVID-period associations remain positive. The negative interactions for foreign executive representation and managerial interlocks remain statistically significant across alternative estimators, whereas the female-representation interaction is less robust. While the stable-period managerial–ownership polynomial is not jointly significant, its COVID interactions are so, indicating a regime difference in the polynomial association. Results are insensitive to governance-variable winsorisation but sensitive to the treatment of extreme Tobin’s Q values. Practical implications Observable governance profiles may carry valuation-relevant information, whose relevance varies across economic conditions. Our findings may inform how firms communicate governance arrangements but do not identify the investor mechanisms driving the observed regime differences. Originality/value The study documents regime-contingent valuation associations attached to structurally persistent governance profiles in an emerging EU capital market and evaluates them through an ESG accountability-signalling lens without excluding competing governance explanations.

title: Navigating Climate Risk for Resilience: A Roadmap of Research Patterns and Emerging Trends
summary: ABSTRACT Climate risk has become a defining challenge for business strategy, yet its research landscape remains fragmented across disciplines. This study maps the intellectual structure of climate risk research through a bibliometric analysis enriched with latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) topic modeling of 2715 peer‐reviewed articles. Our analysis first identifies the following six consolidated research patterns: (1) climate adaptation and community resilience, (2) climate risk and insurance mechanisms, (3) climate finance and green investment, (4) climate extremes and scenario modeling, (5) climate impacts and agricultural resilience, and (6) climate mitigation and energy transition. Analysis of the 2020–2024 literature reveals four emerging trends: urban climate adaptation, climate risk and financial stability, extreme climate events and climate modeling, agriculture, food security and household security. The findings indicate a shift toward integrated approaches connecting the physical, social, and financial dimensions of climate risk. The resulting roadmap identifies converging risks and strategic priorities for organizational resilience while providing policymakers with an evolving evidence base to support climate governance and informed decision‐making under deepening uncertainty.

title: A Study on the Value Creation Pathways of Management Accounting in the Context of Digital Transformation: A Case Study of Midea Group
summary: Within the background of the digital economy, digital transformation has driven the accounting function to extend from traditional external financial disclosure to internal operational decision-making, making management accounting a pivotal tool for manufacturing enterprises to achieve value creation. The home appliance industry is highly competitive, with significant pressure on cost and inventory control; the effectiveness of digital management accounting practices directly impacts the operational quality of home appliance enterprises. This research selects Midea Group, a digital benchmark in the home appliance industry, for case analysis. With the theory of technology empowerment, drawing on core literature on digital management accounting and combining the TOE framework, this paper examines Midea Group’s implementation path for management accounting tools during its digital transformation, analyzes the effectiveness of these implementations and existing shortcomings, and proposes optimization recommendations based on these findings. Meanwhile, this paper aims to provide practical guidance for domestic manufacturing enterprises of a similar nature in implementing digital management accounting. It also contributes to the body of case study evidence on digital management accounting in the home appliance industry.

title: Carbon accounting in the supply chain: investigating its antecedents and consequences for organizations
summary: Over the past decade, stakeholder attention to carbon accounting has intensified, with particular emphasis on greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from firms’ direct operations (Scope 1) and purchased energy use (Scope 2). However, a substantial portion of emissions occurs beyond these boundaries, and firms continue to struggle to identify, measure, and manage emissions embedded in their supply bases. Limited data availability, voluntary disclosure, and supplier heterogeneity significantly impede accurate assessment of supply chain emissions. This paper addresses these challenges by (a) identifying the key drivers of GHG emissions in a firm’s supply base and (b) developing a novel empirical approach to measure supply base emissions. Using data from 1,142 firms and drawing on transaction cost and network theory, we show that greater geographical and industrial diversity significantly increases supply base emissions, and that buyer network influence and supply base interconnectedness moderate these effects.

title: Driving Green Growth through Fintech Innovation: Examining the Moderating Role of Cryptocurrency Integration among NGOs in Malaysia
summary: The current study intends to examine the moderating effect of cryptocurrency integration on the relationship between FinTech-enabled financing methods and green growth among Malaysian environmental NGOs. The analysis focuses on two financing methods, green financing and crowdfunding. A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted, and 151 usable responses were obtained from knowledgeable personnel from 48 registered and active environmental NGOs in Malaysia. The structural analyses were performed using SmartPLS 4. The findings show a significant positive relationship between green financing and green growth whereas the relationship between crowdfunding and green growth was not statistically significant. Cryptocurrency integration was not directly related to green growth at the 5% significance level. The interaction between cryptocurrency integration and green financing was significant and negative, indicating that the positive green financing-green growth association was weaker at higher levels of cryptocurrency integration. The corresponding interaction with crowdfunding was positive, but not statistically significant. Thus, green financing provides the clearest direct contribution to green growth among environmental NGOs, while cryptocurrency integration should be approached with caution as part of a broader strategy that takes into account governance, transparency, regulatory compliance, and environmental sustainability.

title: Power Beyond Organizational Boundaries: Sustainable Supply Chain Management and External Evaluation Consistency
summary: ABSTRACT Sustainable supply chain management (SSCM) is an important vertical governance mechanism transcending organizational boundaries. Previous studies have primarily emphasized its contribution to sustainable performance, while its role as a firm‐manageable dimension relevant to external evaluation consistency remains underexplored. Using 10,656 firm‐year observations from Chinese A‐share listed firms during 2009–2023, this study constructs a text‐based multidimensional co‐occurrence measure of SSCM and examines its association with rating divergence. Results show that stronger SSCM is associated with lower ESG rating divergence, with evidence consistent with information quality and vertical relationship governance channels. The association is stronger for internal‐process and customer‐related SSCM. Divergence is associated with lower risk‐taking propensity and higher supply‐chain cost sharing, while these adverse relationships are weaker at higher SSCM levels. This study extends research by highlighting SSCM as a firm‐manageable dimension associated with greater evaluation consistency. It also highlights SSCM's potential to limit the adverse consequences of persistent rating disagreement.

title: The Accounting Frontier of Biodiversity: A Socio-Economic Critique of ESG Reporting Frameworks and the Promise of Ecological Debt
summary: Purpose – This article examines whether contemporary ESG biodiversity reporting frameworks can fulfill their stated objective of making nature visible, comparable, and governable within economic and financial systems.Methodology – The study adopts a critical qualitative approach grounded in the sociology of quantification and neo-institutional theory. It analyzes the main biodiversity reporting frameworks, including GRI, TNFD, and ESRS E4.Findings – Biodiversity emerges as a boundary object whose complexity, locality, and irreversibility challenge the standardization logic required by financial reporting. Existing frameworks tend to produce a form of “narrated biodiversity” that primarily serves institutional legitimacy rather than effective ecological stewardship.Conclusions – The article argues for a shift toward an ecological debt perspective inspired by the CARE model. By recognizing ecosystem maintenance obligations within accounting systems, this approach offers a more robust framework for ecological accountability and sustainability governanceKeywords: Biodiversity accounting; ESG reporting; institutional legitimacy; CARE model; ecological debt.JEL Codes: M41; Q51; Q56; Q57; G34.

title: Pengaruh Pengetahuan Investasi, Persepsi Risiko, dan Persepsi Return Terhadap Minat Mahasiswa Berinvestasi di Pasar Modal Dengan Persepsi Menabung Sebagai Variabel Moderasi (Studi Kasus Pada Mahasiswa Fakultas Ekonomi dan Bisnis di Kota Mataram)
summary: This study aims to examine the effect of investment knowledge, investment risk perception, and return perception on students’ investment interest in the capital market, with Saving Perception as a moderating variable among students of the Faculty of Economics and Business in Mataram City. The study employed a quantitative approach using a survey method. A total of 106 respondents were selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire with a five-point Likert scale and analyzed using Moderated Regression Analysis (MRA) with IBM SPSS Statistics 26. The results show that investment knowledge and investment risk perception do not significantly affect students’ investment interest. In contrast, return perception has a positive and significant effect on investment interest. Saving Perception also has a positive and significant direct effect on investment interest. However, the interaction terms between investment knowledge and Saving Perception, investment risk perception and Saving Perception, and return perception and Saving Perception are not significant.

title: Pengaruh Green Financing, Environmental Disclosure, dan Kinerja Keuangan terhadap Nilai Perusahaan pada Sektor Basic Materials yang Terdaftar di Bursa Efek Indonesia Periode 2022-2024
summary: This study aims to analyze the effect of green financing, environmental disclosure, and financial performance on firm value in Basic Materials sector companies listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange during the 2022–2024 period. Firm value was measured using Tobin's Q, green financing was measured using Green Coin Rating (GCR), environmental disclosure was measured using the GRI Standards environmental disclosure index, and financial performance was measured using Return on Assets (ROA). This study employed a quantitative approach with secondary data obtained from companies' annual reports and sustainability reports. The sample was selected using purposive sampling, resulting in 28 companies with 63 observations after excluding 21 outlier observations. Data were analyzed using multiple linear regression with the assistance of IBM SPSS Statistics 22. The results show that green financing has no significant effect on firm value (coefficient 0.076; significance 0.789). Environmental disclosure also has no significant effect on firm value (coefficient 0.417; significance 0.126). Financial performance proxied by ROA has no significant effect on firm value either (coefficient 0.859; significance 0.244). The Adjusted R Square value of 0.007 indicates that the three independent variables are only able to explain 0.7% of the variation in firm value, while the remaining 99.3% is explained by other factors outside the research model.

title: THE EFFECT OF INTELLECTUAL CAPITAL AND ESG DISCLOSURE ON FIRM VALUE FROM A SUSTAINABLE VALUE CREATION PERSPECTIVE
summary: This study examines the effects of intellectual capital and environmental, social, and governance (ESG) disclosure on firm value from a sustainable value creation perspective among companies in the consumer non-cyclicals subsector listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange during 2021–2025. The study employed a quantitative approach using secondary data from 20 sampled companies, comprising 100 initial observations and 86 final observations following data processing and first-difference transformation. Multiple linear regression analysis was conducted using SPSS version 25. The results indicate that intellectual capital has a positive and statistically significant individual effect on firm value (t = 5.573; p = 0.000), suggesting that the efficient management of intellectual resources contributes to internal value creation. In contrast, ESG disclosure does not have a statistically significant individual effect on firm value (t = −0.730; p = 0.468). This finding suggests that sustainability transparency is not immediately reflected in short-term market valuation, although it may contribute to organizational legitimacy and long-term risk mitigation. The joint effect of intellectual capital and ESG disclosure on firm value is statistically significant (F = 15.913; p = 0.000), with an adjusted R² of 0.262. The findings highlight the importance of aligning internal intellectual capabilities with external sustainability transparency to support sustainable firm value creation.

title: Islamic Banking Innovation: Addressing Fintech Challenges Through Blue Ocean Strategy
summary: Purpose— This study examines Islamic banking innovations to address fintech challenges through a blue ocean strategy. Therefore, the main focus of the discussion is on: External business environment factors of Islamic banking; Internal business environment factors; SWOT analysis; and Blue Ocean Strategy. Design/methodology/approach— This descriptive qualitative research used primary data collected through interviews and secondary data. Five Islamic commercial banks were selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected, reduced, and then triangulated using literature and documentation studies to strengthen arguments and analysis, leading to strategic and innovative recommendations. Findings— The strategy of Islamic banks in responding to fintech challenges focuses on holistic digital transformation to achieve operational efficiency, increased security, Sharia compliance, and the creation of a holistic digital service ecosystem, such as: integrating various financial services, ZISWAF platforms and disaster mitigation, cardless withdrawals, investment services, legacy management, and halal supply chain financing in one holistic ecosystem supported by partnerships with industry and government. Research implication/limitation— This study develops an integrated digital ecosystem model for Islamic banking based on Blue Ocean Strategy, emphasizing value innovation amidst fintech disruption. Unlike previous studies that focused on digitalization and operational efficiency, this study offers a strategic framework that integrates sharia principles, digital transformation, and differentiation strategies to create new competitive advantages. Thus this study expands the literature on Islamic banking digital transformation through a Blue Ocean Strategy perspective and provides a conceptual framework for strengthening competitiveness in the fintech era. Originality/value— A weakness of this study is its limited representation of the broader and rapidly evolving dynamics of the Islamic finance and fintech markets, due to the limited data used and the specific sample size. However this study provides useful initial insights, and therefore requires multiple approaches to build a more robust and comprehensive body of knowledge that provides a complete or definitive picture of the complex and ever-changing Islamic finance and fintech landscape.

title: Bira 91: governance, debt, and the challenge of founder control
summary: Learning outcomes The key learning objectives of this case study are as follows: Case overview/synopsis This case examines Bira 91, an Indian craft-beer and premium alcoholic beverage company, during a period of rapid growth, rising financial pressure and governance transition between 2020 and late 2025. Founded by Ankur Jain in 2015, Bira 91 developed into one of India’s most visible youth-oriented beer brands through its distinctive positioning, strong urban appeal, investor-backed expansion and a premium craft-beer identity. However, as the company expanded its production capacity, distribution network and market presence, it also faced rising debt, working-capital pressure, lender scrutiny and investor concern over governance discipline. The protagonist, Ankur Jain, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Bira 91, faces a critical board-level dilemma. He must decide whether to step aside in favour of professional leadership, retain his position while accepting stronger governance and financial controls or preserve the existing founder-led structure while attempting refinancing and operational recovery. The case is designed to teach corporate governance, entrepreneurial finance, venture debt, capital-structure discipline, stakeholder management and leadership transition in founder-led emerging-market startups. Complexity academic level This case is suitable for postgraduate management education, particularly MBA, Executive MBA and specialised master’s programmes. It can also be used in doctoral seminars dealing with entrepreneurial finance, corporate governance, emerging-market firms and founder-led organisations. Subject code CSS 1: Accounting and Finance.

title: Adaptive Labor Infrastructure for AI Disruption: The Hybrid Agora: collective meta-intelligence, human-agent teams and a virtuous learning circle between communities and machines
summary: Artificial intelligence already performs much of the repetitive cognitive work in closed domains faster and at lower cost. The policy and research conversation now asks how workers and AI build expertise together, whether reskilling and reemployment can scale at the pace of disruption, and what public and private investment in workforce transitions actually delivers. This paper addresses a question those agendas leave open: where, with whom and for what purpose a person whose work is changing retrains, and what the human community and the machine can learn from each other in the process. It proposes an Adaptive Labor Infrastructure for AI disruption (ALI): a territorial system whose unit is the Collective Meta-intelligence Center (CMC), conceived as a hybrid agora — the oral, dialogic and peripatetic space of the classical city, updated with AI agents as team members and with measured outcomes. The paper makes five nameable contributions. (1) It reformulates Sternberg et al.’s (2021) individual meta-intelligence as a group property with two axes, capacity and orientation, whose product, vital lucidity, is measurable. (2) It defines a testable results chain: lucidity → purpose → self- actualization → social cohesion → positive social impact, with an externally validated instrument for each link. (3) It states the inversion of the valuable profile: dispersed, transversal and self-taught profiles, penalized by specialization-based selection, become the most valuable once specialized execution is performed by agents. (4) It describes a virtuous circle of bidirectional learning: people learn from multi-agent systems to work as interconnected agents without losing individuality; systems learn from community deliberation, with affected parties present and interests declared, a holistic judgment of the common good that preference data cannot capture. (5) It proposes computational linguistics of cohesion as an intersection field between cognitive science, natural language processing and applied ethics. The paper situates itself academically (§0), translates its constructs into the vocabulary of AI-and-work research funders and of corporate social responsibility and ESG reporting (§15), and states the value it offers to employers, consultancies and AI developers (§16). It deploys one method in three contexts — work, academia and science — and lists eleven falsifiable hypotheses. Limitations, including the author’s conflict of interest and instrumental circularity, are declared.

title: Interside: Blockchain Interoperability Architecture for Supply Chain Tracking
summary: Modern supply chains rely on permissioned blockchain networks that frequently operate as isolated entities, resulting in fragmented data, limited visibility, and inconsistent governance. This research addresses these challenges by proposing “Interside,” an interoperability framework designed explicitly for multi-network supply chain ecosystems. Using a design science research methodology, the study includes requirement analysis, framework development, prototype implementation, and a preliminary evaluation. The architecture features a main-chain/side-chain model that preserves network autonomy while enabling secure, auditable cross-chain communication and selective data sharing via a dedicated side-chain tracking ledger. A prototype was built with Hyperledger Fabric and Weaver components, and the framework was evaluated through a conceptual comparison with direct and hub-based approaches. Results show that Interside improves decentralization, governance autonomy, and auditability compared with existing models, with minor trade-offs in prototype performance. This work introduces a novel architectural blueprint for permissioned blockchain interoperability in supply chain environments and outlines practical directions for future large-scale performance benchmarking.

title: Cryptocurrency Adoption and Its Impact on the Traditional Banking System in India
summary: A major innovation in the global financial system, cryptocurrency is posing a threat to the established banking system. Due to the development of fintech platforms, digital awareness, and technological advancements, the use of cryptocurrencies like Ethereum and Bitcoin has grown significantly in India. This study looks at bitcoin adoption and how it affects India's conventional banking sector. It focuses on the ways in which cryptocurrencies affect banking services such financial intermediation, payments, remittances, and client trust. The study's foundation is secondary data gathered from government publications, Reserve Bank of India bulletins, and academic journals. Trends and implications are assessed using descriptive analysis. The results suggest that while cryptocurrencies encourage banks to innovate through digital banking and blockchain adoption, they also present challenges to traditional banks by decreasing transaction reliance. The study comes to the conclusion that risk management and sustainable financial development depend on a balanced regulatory environment.

title: Digital Transformation in Vietnam: Opportunities, Barriers, and Policy Implications for Sustainable Development
summary: This structured narrative review examines the opportunities, barriers, and policy implications of digital transformation in Vietnam during 2020–2026. It integrates peer-reviewed studies of organizational change and digital strategy with Vietnamese policy instruments, official economic statistics, the United Nations E-Government Survey, and regional digital-market reports. The National Statistics Office estimated that digital-economy value added accounted for 14.02% of GDP in 2025 (approximately US$72.1 billion), while Vietnam ranked 71st of 193 countries in the 2024 UN E-Government Development Index. Major enabling conditions include sustained policy commitment, expanding digital connectivity, and demand for online services. Principal barriers include uneven digital capabilities, fragmented data governance, limited small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) resources, cybersecurity exposure, and disparities in meaningful access. The review proposes a six-domain policy framework combining institutional coordination, interoperability, human capital, SME support, trust and security, and outcome-based evaluation. As a narrative synthesis, it does not claim systematic coverage or causal identification.

title: Invisible Brokers, Visible Haze: Value Chains and the Political Ecology of Northern Thailand’s Maize Economy
summary: Each dry season, thick haze blankets northern Thailand. Maize cultivation, driven largely by demand for animal feed, is one of its most politically contested sources. Policy responses often target farmers through burning bans, technical fixes, and behavioural change campaigns. This article focuses on the middlemen who link upland maize fields to downstream feed markets. It shows that brokers, traders, and silo operators, by controlling access to credit, logistics, and markets, translate corporate demand, price volatility, and regulatory pressures into everyday farming practices. Moral economies of debt, reciprocity, and patronage intersect with buyer-driven value chain pressures to shape brokerage practices and disperse accountability for environmental harm. These practices reinforce farmers’ dependence on maize, and make burning appear the most viable option while displacing responsibility onto farmers and shielding large agribusinesses. The article demonstrates that market power operates through everyday social relations of credit, trust, and loyalty to reproduce unequal commodity relations. This helps explain why haze persists despite repeated policy interventions. The article integrates middlemen into environmental governance analyses, shows that value chain governance and moral economy combine to reproduce environmental injustice, and contributes to meatways scholarship, tracing the intermediary networks through which national and regional meat demand reproduces environmental harm.

title: Digital Transformation and Energy Poverty Alleviation: Heterogeneous Transmission of Sub Dimensions of Urban-Rural Integration
summary: Energy poverty has become a major issue that impedes social equity, exacerbates the wealth gap, and constrains China’s modernization process. The rapid development of the digital economy and urban–rural integration has provided new pathways to address this challenge. This study adopts urban–rural integration as its research perspective, utilizes panel data from various provinces in China spanning from 2013 to 2023, and employs a mediation and moderation effect model to systematically examine the impact of the digital economy on energy poverty, its underlying mechanisms, and its heterogeneous characteristics. The research findings indicate that the digital economy can significantly alleviate energy poverty. The mediation mechanism of urban–rural integration reveals that spatial integration and non-agricultural employment serve as the primary transmission channels through which the digital economy mitigates energy poverty, whereas industrial integration may instead exacerbate energy poverty by reducing energy consumption levels. Heterogeneity analysis demonstrates that the energy poverty alleviation effects of the digital economy are stronger in low-income provinces, provinces with high energy intensity, and resource-based provinces. This study contributes to scientifically clarifying the causal relationships among the digital economy, urban–rural integration, and energy poverty, thereby providing a reference framework for developing countries of similar types to address structural contradictions arising from urban–rural dual structures and energy poverty governance.

title: Water Ecological Civilization Pilots and Corporate Water Pollution in China: Evidence from Listed Firms
summary: This study examines the causal effect of China's Water Ecological Civilization Pilot Program (WECPP) on corporate water pollutant emissions. Ecological civilization, as formally embedded in China's national governance framework, represents a systematic strategy integrating environmental protection into economic and social development through institutional design, regulatory enforcement, and resource stewardship. Exploiting the staggered rollout of pilot city designations as a quasi-natural experiment and employing a difference-in-differences estimator on a sample of listed firms over the period 2007 to 2022, we document that pilot designation induces a significant and robust reduction in corporate water pollutant emissions. This finding survives an extensive battery of robustness and validity checks. Mediation analyses provide evidence consistent with three potential pathways: enhanced environmental enforcement, increased public environmental attention, and improved internal green management practices. Heterogeneity analyses reveal that the emission-reducing effect is more pronounced in regions subject to greater governance pressure, among firms with weaker ex ante environmental awareness, and in firms with greater climate-risk exposure. Furthermore, the program induces unintended spatial responses, as some firms react to heightened regulatory oversight through geographic relocation, which is consistent with possible geographic reallocation of pollution-intensive activities across regions. These findings offer actionable implications for advancing ecological civilization, optimizing environmental governance arrangements, and designing cooperative regulatory frameworks to mitigate pollution displacement across jurisdictions.

title: Supply Chain Collaboration in Baijiu Enterprises amid Digital and Intelligent Transformation: Challenges and Optimization Strategies
summary: The Baijiu industry is changing its structure. This change shows limits in old supply chain management. The limits are in information sharing, production-sales coordination, inventory management, and risk response. Digital and intelligent transformation gives Baijiu firms new ways to solve these problems and improve supply chain efficiency. This study uses supply chain cooperation theory and dynamic capability theory. It uses a literature review and analytical synthesis. It looks at key supply chain problems in Baijiu. These problems come from long production cycles, strong reliance on traditional brewing, and changing market demand. Then it studies how digital and intelligent transformation helps supply chain cooperation through three mechanisms: information sharing, resource integration, and dynamic response. Then the study gives optimization strategies. These strategies are: build an integrated information-sharing system; improve production-sales coordination; strengthen resource integration between organizations; and improve supply chain risk management. The analysis shows that effective supply chain change depends on digital technology adoption. It also depends on combining data and organizational capabilities to support cooperation across the supply chain. These efforts can improve operating efficiency, strengthen supply chain resilience, and increase value creation. This study gives practical ideas for Baijiu firms and for digital and intelligent transformation in traditional industries.

title: A Study on The Evolving Financial Landscape, Risk Dynamics and Institutional Integration of Cryptocurrency in India
summary: Abstract The rapid development of cryptocurrency and blockchain technology has significantly influenced the global financial landscape, creating new opportunities for digital financial innovation while introducing various financial, technological, and regulatory challenges. This study examines the evolving financial landscape of cryptocurrency in India, with particular emphasis on risk dynamics and institutional integration. It explores the development of Virtual Digital Assets (VDAs), the major risks associated with cryptocurrency, and the regulatory mechanisms introduced by the Government of India and financial authorities. The study focuses on market volatility, cybersecurity threats, consumer protection, money laundering, financial stability, taxation, and Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing (AML/CFT) compliance. It also examines the growing relationship between cryptocurrency-related activities, financial institutions, fintech organisations, and India's broader digital-finance ecosystem. The research adopts a secondary and descriptive analytical approach based on publications from the Reserve Bank of India, the Income Tax Department, the Financial Intelligence Unit–India, the Bank for International Settlements, and other credible sources. The study highlights the importance of balancing technological innovation with effective regulation, risk management, and consumer protection. It concludes that a transparent and well-structured regulatory framework is essential for addressing cryptocurrency-related risks and supporting the responsible development of India's digital financial ecosystem.

title: Developing an Eco-Nationalism-Based Village Regulatory Model for SDG Achievement and Sustainable Local Economic Development in Madura, Indonesia
summary: Sustainable local economic development at the village level requires a balance between community welfare, environmental protection, and effective local governance. In Madura, the use of natural resources remains insufficiently aligned with environmental carrying capacity, creating challenges for achieving sustainable village development and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). This study aims to develop an eco-nationalism-based village regulatory model that integrates environmental protection, sustainable local economic development, and SDG implementation within village governance. Employing an empirical juridical approach, the study draws on village regulations, interviews, field observations, literature, and relevant governance documents to examine regulatory practices, institutional capacity, and community legal behavior. The findings identify four interconnected components of the proposed model: (1) strengthening environmental protection provisions in village regulations, (2) fostering ecological legal awareness and community participation, (3) promoting local economic activities based on environmental carrying capacity, and (4) strengthening village institutions for SDG implementation. The model positions village regulations as a strategic legal instrument for integrating ecological values, national identity, and sustainable local economic development. The study contributes to the development of village-level environmental governance by demonstrating how eco-nationalism can provide a normative and institutional foundation for translating environmental stewardship into local regulatory practice. The findings also highlight the need for regulatory drafting assistance, capacity building for village governments, and institutionalized community participation to ensure effective implementation. This model offers a context-sensitive framework for strengthening sustainable village development in Madura and other rural areas facing similar ecological and socioeconomic challenges.

title: A Study of the Dual Facets of Third-Party Logistics Partnerships: Opportunities and Risks in Modern Supply Chains
summary: This paper explores the opportunities, risks, and rewards of companies outsourcing functions, specifically supply chain or logistics functions through an outside entity or a third-party provider. Today’s markets are global in nature, and to be competitive in this global market, companies have to make critical decisions, including the outsourcing of some, if not all, of their supply chain or logistics functions. Outsourcing is a decision that should be approached carefully, as its benefits might not outweigh its costs. The outsourcing proposition has to make sense in various aspects, not only cost, as companies have to balance more than one type of shareholder, as they have ESG commitments (Environmental, Social and Governance) to account for. Plus; off the heels of the recent COVID-19 pandemic, selecting a reliable third- party logistics provider (3PL) is more important than ever to navigate similar future events or other natural disasters that disrupt supply chains.

title: Shared Stakes, Shared Brains: Common Ownership and Inventor Mobility Along Supply Chains
summary: ABSTRACT Research Question/Issue This study investigates the influence of common ownership on inventor mobility along supply chains and examines its role in shaping the interfirm governance conditions for human‐capital reallocation within portfolios. Research Findings/Insights Using Chinese listed supplier–customer pairs from 2012 to 2023, we find that inventors are more likely to move along supply chains when common owners hold larger stakes in both suppliers and customers. Through mechanism tests, we reveal that common owners increase the likelihood of such flows by facilitating collaboration and information exchange. This effect is more evident when common owners are long‐term, institutional, or state‐owned, and when supply chains have a weaker collaborative culture, less efficient management, or a poorer legal environment. Finally, such flows mainly increase incremental innovation and enhance innovation performance of both supply‐chain partners. Theoretical/Academic Implications This study extends research on inventor mobility from competitors to collaborators and identifies common ownership as a governance determinant of supply‐chain human‐capital flows. It also reframes common ownership's labor‐market effects from horizontal anticompetition to vertical human‐capital reallocation and highlights inventor mobility along supply chains as a person‐level channel for complementary knowledge recombination, rather than another collaboration‐style outcome. Practitioner/Policy Implications Our findings suggest that investors can leverage common ownership to enhance portfolio competitiveness by strengthening the governance conditions that support inventor mobility. For policymakers, particularly those in emerging markets, our results demonstrate that common ownership can fill institutional voids and alleviate supply‐chain frictions, suggesting that regulatory frameworks should recognize its benefits in supporting human‐capital reallocation and supply‐chain resilience.

title: Fossil-fuel subsidy reform as a step towards a just transition: a litmus test for COP31
summary: International efforts to mobilise private capital for low-carbon development coexist with widespread government support for fossil fuels in economies accounting for a large majority of global energy supply. By lowering the cost of producing or consuming fossil energy, this support alters relative returns in favour of carbon-intensive activities. This article assesses the implications of this distortion for implementing Article 2.1(c) of the Paris Agreement, which calls for finance flows to be made consistent with low-emission and climate-resilient development. It argues that fossil-fuel-subsidy reform is therefore not solely a fiscal or energy-policy issue but also a matter of policy coherence in implementing this finance-alignment objective. The evidence reviewed also shows that, in most cases, broad price support is poorly targeted and regressive in distribution: higher-income households obtain larger absolute benefits because they consume more energy. Against this background, the article develops a three-part litmus test for COP31: progressive reform of fossil-fuel support to strengthen policy coherence under Article 2.1(c), transparent disclosure that permits progress to be tracked over time and protection of vulnerable households as part of a just transition. To operationalise these tests, the article proposes that Parties agree at COP31 to prepare nationally determined fossil-fuel-subsidy reform plans, modelled on the Paris Agreement’s nationally determined contributions (NDCs) and submitted alongside successive NDCs.

title: From responsibility to reputation: how perceived corporate social responsibility shapes corporate brand image
summary: Purpose This study aims to examine how perceived corporate social responsibility (PCSR) shapes corporate brand image by unpacking the psychological mechanisms and boundary conditions underlying this relationship in the telecommunications service sector. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on the Stimulus–Organism–Response framework, this study develops an integrated moderated–mediation model in which brand familiarity and brand equity function as cognitive and affective mediators respectively, and customer trust operates as a key boundary condition. Survey data from 350 customers of leading telecommunications providers in India were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling. Findings The results show that PCSR has a non-significant direct effect on corporate brand image and indirect effects through both brand familiarity and brand equity, indicating complementary full mediation. PCSR strengthens brand familiarity by enhancing cognitive accessibility and recognition, while simultaneously increasing brand equity through value based and emotional evaluations. Customer trust significantly moderates these relationships, amplifying the branding effects of perceived CSR under high trust and weakening them when trust is low. Practical implications The findings highlight the importance of treating PCSR as a strategic, trust anchored branding capability rather than a symbolic reputation tool, particularly in service intensive and trust sensitive markets. Originality/value By combining dual mediation and trust based moderation, this study provides a holistic and decision relevant understanding of how PCSR translates into corporate brand image, reflective of quality the brand offers.

title: Conflict Management through Corporate Social Responsibility in Shell, NNPC and Chevron in Delta and Rivers States
summary: This study examined the conflict management through Corporate Social Responsibility Programmes of Shell, NNPC and Chevron in Delta and Rivers States. The objectives were among others to find out the extent unfulfilled Corporate Social Responsibility obligations may have caused conflicts between Shell, NNPC Chevron and the host communities in Delta and Rivers States, Nigeria. The frustration-aggression theory was adopted. The research design adopted for this study was the descriptive survey design. The population of this study is made up two streams, the public relations units and departments of the oil companies and the residents of the communities where the companies operate. For the oil companies, Shell, NNPC and Chevron, the public relations staff 145. The population of the residents of the communities of the two states, Rivers and Delta States was 145 from the oil companies and 1,841,110 from the host communities the population of the study with the total 1,841,255. The sample size for the study is 384 according to Krejcie and Morgan sample table. The sampling techniques used in this study were multi-stage cluster and purposive. The researcher obtained the data for this study using questionnaire and interview guide. The researcher adopted quantitative and qualitative methods to present and analyze the data gathered from the respondents. The finding revealed that the extent unfulfilled CSR obligations responsible for the conflicts between Shell, NNPC and Chevron, and the host communities in Delta and Rivers State were high extent. The host communities accepted that the extent of unfulfilled CSR obligations responsible for the conflicts between Shell, NNPC and Chevron and the host communities in Delta and Rivers State were a high. The study concluded that a concerning trend wherein unfulfilled CSR obligations have led to conflicts between the multinational oil companies and their respective host communities. The study recommended that it is imperative for Shell, NNPC and Chevron to prioritise their CSR commitments, engage in meaningful dialogue with community stakeholders and implement transparent accountability mechanisms to ensure the fulfilment of promises.

title: Digital Trade Restrictions and High-Technology Export Performance: Panel Fixed Effects Evidence from Emerging Economies
summary: As the digital economy transforms global trade, cross-border data flows and digital service inputs have become critical for technology-intensive manufacturing. This study examines the relationship between digital trade restrictiveness and high-technology export performance across 20 emerging economies from 2014 to 2024. Employing a country fixed-effects estimator and a set of robustness specifications addressing alternative error structures and common temporal shocks, the analysis investigates whether the OECD Digital Services Trade Restrictiveness Index (Digital STRI) is systematically associated with the share of high-technology exports in manufactured exports. The baseline country fixed-effects estimate is negative and statistically significant, indicating that higher levels of Digital STRI are associated with lower high-technology export shares. Across alternative covariance estimators and Two-Way Fixed Effects specifications, the estimated coefficient remains negative and similar in magnitude, although its statistical precision varies across inference procedures. Economic maturity, proxied by GDP per capita, is positively and significantly associated with the high-technology export share in the baseline specification, whereas foreign direct investment (FDI), manufacturing value added (MVA), and trade openness are statistically insignificant in that specification. The results are interpreted as conditional associations rather than causal effects and highlight the potential relevance of open and interoperable digital regulatory environments for technology-intensive export performance.

title: Drivers of Sustainability Strategy Adoption in European SMEs : The Role of Digitalisation, Innovation and Organisational Barriers
summary: ABSTRACT Sustainability has become a core concern to be embedded in firms' strategic orientations. This study investigates how digitalisation, innovation, and internal organisational barriers contribute to or constrain the development of formal sustainability‐oriented strategies in SMEs. In addition, it examines whether internal barriers to innovation moderate the relationship between different innovation types and the adoption of formal sustainability strategies. The paper applies a binary logistic regression model to microdata from Flash Eurobarometer 486, using a final analytical sample of 11,861 SMEs across 35 European countries. The research reveals that product, organisational, and marketing innovation, as well as factors associated with digitalisation, are positively and significantly associated with the probability of SMEs adopting a formal sustainability strategy. Previous participation in sustainability practices shows a positive and statistically significant relationship as well. Although the coefficient for internal barriers is not statistically significant among firms reporting none of the three innovation types, barriers weaken the positive association between marketing innovation and sustainability strategy adoption. This finding is supported by both the log‐odds and probability‐scale analyses. These findings highlight how innovation, digitalisation, and organisational constraints are associated with the formalisation of sustainability strategies in SMEs. The primary contribution of this study is to integrate the themes of digital transformation, innovation, and sustainability within a strategic management framework. By empirically analysing European SME behaviour across the EU, this research addresses an underexplored intersection in the literature, offering robust evidence on how internal drivers and barriers affect the formalisation of sustainability strategies. The results offer a theoretical understanding and practical application for managers and policymakers seeking to promote sustainable change among SMEs.

title: The Empty Occupant: A Reading Guide for Undergraduates
summary: This reading guide accompanies Nicholas Cott’s monograph The Empty Occupant: Answerability, Testimony, and the Limits of Machine-Mediated Authority (manuscript dated 28 October 2026). It is written for undergraduates with no background in philosophy, law or computing. The guide teaches the monograph’s framework in ten lessons. Topics include: the four relations of Answerability, the four occupancy statuses, and the principle that missing bearership is not defective ownership; when automated review counts as genuine reconsideration; the testimonial value of machine output, and when an institution may adopt it (Normative Sponsorship); Deontic Debt and Institutional Insolvency; the real cases the book examines (Robodebt, Moffatt v. Air Canada, TennCare, Post Office Horizon, the Dutch childcare-benefits affair and DPD) and its invented Meridian–Aster case; practical recourse and auditing, and the main rival theories. A single invented running case, the Northvale rent-assistance council, is built up lesson by lesson into a complete analysis. Worked examples train students to keep distinct verdicts apart: causal contribution, legal liability, commitment ownership, warranted adoption and adequate discharge. They also teach students to separate what a record shows from what it leaves undetermined. Each lesson includes learning objectives, key-term definitions, common mistakes, a summary and discussion questions. The guide also provides: an eight-step method for new cases, with two practice cases; fifteen multiple-choice questions, each explaining why the tempting wrong answers are wrong; eight essay questions; a twelve-week course plan; answers to all lesson questions; a quick-reference section and a glossary. Section references follow the 28 October 2026 manuscript. Statements about legal and documentary status follow the monograph and are current as of 10 October 2026. Northvale and the two practice cases are invented for teaching and describe no real organisation. This guide was drafted with AI assistance.

title: "Digital transformation in accountancy: a study of emerging technologies, adoption challenges, and future implications"
summary: Abstract The field of accountancy has undergone a paradigm shift in the last two decades due to rapid technological advancements. Traditional bookkeeping and manual ledger systems have been replaced by cloud-based accounting software, artificial intelligence, blockchain, and data analytics tools. This paper explores the integration of technology in accountancy, examining how automation, AI-driven audit tools, cloud ERP systems, and blockchain are redefining accounting practices. It further analyses the benefits such as enhanced accuracy, real-time reporting, fraud detection, and cost efficiency, alongside challenges including cybersecurity risks, skill gaps, and resistance to change. The study employs a mixed-method approach, reviewing secondary literature and industry reports from 2020-2026 to assess technology adoption trends among small, medium, and large enterprises in India. Findings suggest that while large firms have embraced digital transformation, MSMEs lag due to cost and awareness barriers. The paper concludes that technology in accountancy is no longer optional but a strategic necessity, recommending continuous upskilling, regulatory support, and phased digital adoption for sustainable growth.

title: Internal security in the digital age – challenges and development areas
summary: The aim of this article is to present and systematise contemporary directions in the development of internal security in the context of advancing digital transformation. The subject of the study is the impact of digital technologies on the nature of internal threats and on the functioning of institutions responsible for ensuring state security. The article has a review-analytical character. The study employs a review of the relevant literature, an analysis of legal acts and strategic documents. The author compared the solutions for application of digital technologies in the field of security adopted in different countries and international organisations. The conducted analysis demonstrates that the development of these technologies has fundamentally transformed internal security systems, requiring changes in management models, the development of interinstitutional cooperation, and the adaptation of legal frameworks to emerging threats. In the conclusions, the author indicates that effective internal security in the digital age requires an integrated approach combining technological solutions, appropriate legal frameworks, development of institutional capacities, and international cooperation.

title: The Evolution of Rentier Logic of Financialization in the Context of the Digitalization of the Economy
summary: Subject. The evolution of rent logic in the context of economic digitalization, with a focus on its transformation amid financialization. Objectives. To provide a theoretical understanding of rent as a system‑forming element of the modern economy, ensuring the linkage between the processes of distribution, capitalization, and the formation of financial assets. Methods. The study draws on approaches from classical political economy, Marxist and neo‑Ricardian traditions, as well as contemporary concepts of the digital economy and platform capitalism. Results. A conceptual approach to the analysis of the rent logic of financialization has been developed, within which rent is interpreted as a capitalizable income stream that determines the dynamics of asset values and credit relations. The interconnection of various forms of rent – land, spatial, contractual, and digital – is demonstrated as manifestations of a unified logic of income extraction through control over access conditions. It is substantiated that adaptive forms of rent exhibit the properties of quasi‑financial instruments, enabling risk distribution, while affective and cognitive labor serves as a source of digital rent, capitalized in the value of platforms. A distinction has been made between forms of digital rent, reflecting differences in their sources of generation and mechanisms of appropriation. Conclusions and Relevance. Rent logic under conditions of financialization acquires a universal character and transcends individual sectors, thereby shaping the architecture of the modern economy. This implies the need to rethink rent as a category underlying not only distributional but also financial processes, and calls for consideration of its role in the development of economic policy and regulatory instruments. The results will be useful for analyzing financial markets, developing regulatory tools for digital platforms, and designing mechanisms for the redistribution of rental income.

title: Heterogeneous effects of green finance, governance, and geopolitical risk on renewable energy consumption in G7 economies
summary: This study examines the effects of environmental policy stringency, green finance, geopolitical risk, governance, economic growth, and inequalities on renewable energy consumption across G7 economies (2003–2023). Employing Quantile Method of Moments Regression (QMMR) and Dumitrescu–Hurlin causality tests, the analysis captures heterogeneous dynamics across energy transition stages. Findings indicate that policy stringency, green finance, governance quality, and economic growth drive renewable energy consumption, with regulatory and financial mechanisms exerting the strongest impacts at lower-to-middle quantiles. Conversely, geopolitical risk dampens renewable consumption, particularly at higher quantiles due to heightened investment uncertainty and supply chain vulnerabilities. Income and gender inequalities exhibit marginal effects, confirming that institutional capacity and regulatory frameworks predominate in advanced economies. Ultimately, the results underscore the need for stage-differentiated policy mixes integrating green finance, robust governance, and risk mitigation to advance clean energy targets (SDGs 7, 10, and 13).

title: Corporate Social Responsibilities of Oil Transnational Companies, Host Communities and Environmental Dynamics in the Niger Delta Region, Nigeria
summary: Corporate social responsibility (CSR) is a way of given back to the immediate community of the organization. This study therefore analyzed the corporate social responsibility strategies of oil transnational corporations in the Niger Delta region in Nigeria. Data for the study were collected using the library research method (secondary data). Social exchange and frustration aggression theories were applied to guide the study. Study showed that the practice of corporate social responsibility by oil transnational in the Niger Delta were not good enough and as such have not made significant impact in positively affecting the lives of the people and the social and economic development of the host communities. It was recommended among others that the community relations department should be created out of the public relations departments of these oil transnationals companies which would be solely responsible for matters affecting the host communities, especially where such department does not exist; the oil transnational corporations should strive to necessarily seek the full participation of host communities in its corporate social responsibility projects to enable them gain more acceptance from the people whom the projects are meant for; that the oil transnational corporations should engage in projects that have direct impact on the people.

title: Trade Protection along Supply Chains
summary: We study the effects of trade protection along supply chains. We focus on temporary trade barriers against China, which has been the main target of US trade protection during the last decades. To deal with endogeneity concerns, we use an instrumental variable strategy, exploiting changes in the identity of swing states across presidential terms and heterogeneous exposure to these political shocks across industries. We find that politically motivated trade protection generates winners and losers: It fosters employment growth in protected industries but hampers employment growth in downstream industries. Our estimates imply a negative overall impact on US jobs. (JEL D72, F13, F14, L14, O19, P33)

title: Supply Chain Digitalization and Business Performance: The Role of Artificial Intelligence, IoT, and Data Analytics
summary: Supply chain digitalization has emerged as a major component of contemporary business transformation as organizations seek greater visibility, efficiency, resilience, responsiveness, and competitiveness across increasingly complex global supply networks. Artificial intelligence (AI), the Internet of Things (IoT), and data analytics are among the principal technologies driving this transformation. This paper examines the relationship between supply chain digitalization and business performance, focusing specifically on how AI, IoT, and data analytics influence operational efficiency, forecasting accuracy, inventory management, logistics, supply chain visibility, risk management, customer service, resilience, and financial performance. The study adopts a systematic literature review and conceptual analytical approach to synthesize existing theoretical and empirical research. The analysis indicates that AI can strengthen forecasting, optimization, automation, predictive maintenance, supplier assessment, and decision-making; IoT technologies can improve real-time monitoring, traceability, asset utilization, and visibility; and data analytics can transform large volumes of operational information into predictive and prescriptive insights. Their combined use can create digitally integrated supply chains capable of responding more rapidly to market changes and disruptions. However, digital transformation also introduces challenges involving implementation costs, cybersecurity, data quality, legacy-system integration, interoperability, organizational resistance, skills shortages, privacy, and AI governance. The paper proposes an integrated conceptual framework in which AI capability, IoT connectivity, and dataanalytics capability strengthen supply chain visibility, agility, integration, and resilience, which subsequently influence operational and financial performance. The study concludes that technology alone does not guarantee superior business performance; value creation depends on strategic alignment, high-quality data, organizational capabilities, workforce skills, governance, cybersecurity, and effective integration across supply chain partners.

title: MANAJEMEN PENDIDIKAN ISLAM MALAYSIA DALAM MENGHADAPI GLOBALISASI DAN DISRUPSI DIGITAL: KAJIAN PUSTAKA TERHADAP STRATEGI BERKELANJUTAN, SMART MADRASAH, DAN REFORMASI KELEMBAGAAN
summary: Globalization and digital disruption require Islamic educational institutions to rethink how they manage curricula, human resources, and learning services. Malaysia is a compelling case because its Islamic education is integrated into the national education system while religious schools remain in place. This study analyzes the management of Islamic education in Malaysia in responding to globalization and digital disruption, focusing on sustainable strategies, the smart madrasah concept, and institutional reform. It employs a library research method drawing on books, journal articles, and policy documents. The findings show that (1) Islamic education management in Malaysia is guided by strong national policy; (2) digital transformation is directed through the national education blueprint and digital learning platforms; (3) the smart madrasah integrates technology, leadership, and Islamic values; and (4) institutional reform requires harmonizing religious and national schools. These findings offer lessons for developing Islamic education management in Indonesia.

title: The Role of Accounting Information in Financial Market Efficiency: Evidence from Emerging Economies
summary: Accounting information has many roles in the financial market, squeezing the information gap, aiding in investment so as to improve the allocation of financial resources. The role of accounting information in the promotion of the market efficiency, however, differs by country including between developed and emerging economies. This article examines these connections from the accounting information quality, disclosure transparency and earnings information, corporate governance and institutional development perspectives and in relation to the financial markets' efficiency in developing economies. With existing theories and previous empirical studies, the paper adopts a conceptual and literature-based approach of "explanation" to describe the impact of accounting information on the incorporation of firm specific information into security prices. Seeking out from the analysis, it indicates that financial information should be timely, reliable, comparable and transparent, as it can improve the investors' confidence and strengthen the price discovery. But if there is poor legal and regulatory enforcement, high overall and concentrated stock holdings, poor investor protection, non-standard accounting principles, and low financial literacy, then the quality of the data disclosed can be reduced. The article contends that accounting information, by itself, is not sufficient to ensure market efficiency: It's effectiveness relies on the institutional context of its production, disclosure, interpretation and enforcement context. As such, enhancing the quality of accounting standards and audit quality, corporate governance and digital disclosure systems is an imperative for emerging economies aspiring to more transparent and efficient financial markets. The article adds to an understanding of the way in which the institutional setting within which accounting information is produced can assist the efficiency of the market, and points to future empirical studies.

title: From Traditional Universities to Digital Institutions
summary: Universities worldwide are under growing pressure to reinvent themselves as digital institutions, yet the factors that actually drive this shift are rarely examined systematically. title: Audit Committee Financial Expertise and Sustainability Reporting of Listed Deposit Money Banks in Nigeria: Moderated by Women Chairperson
summary: Sustainability reporting has become an integral aspect of corporate governance as stakeholders increasingly demand transparency regarding environmental, social, and governance performance. In the Nigerian banking sector, Deposit Money Banks are strategically positioned to promote sustainable finance; however, sustainability disclosures remain uneven across institutions. This study examines the effect of audit committee financial expertise on sustainability reporting of listed deposit money banks in Nigeria, while assessing the moderating role of audit committee women chairperson. The study adopted an ex‑post facto research design using secondary data extracted from the audited annual reports of all fourteen (14) listed DMBs in Nigeria for the period 2010–2024. Data were analysed using panel regression techniques with the aid of STATA. Findings revealed that audit committee financial expertise has a positive and statistically significant effect on sustainability reporting. The presence of a woman chairperson on the audit committee was also found to significantly enhance sustainability reporting quality. Additionally, the moderating effect of audit committee women chairperson on the relationship between audit committee financial expertise and sustainability reporting was statistically significant. The study concludes that audit committee financial expertise significantly enhances the quality of sustainability reporting among Nigerian deposit money banks. Similarly, audit committee women chairperson contributes positively and does significantly moderate the effect of audit committee financial expertise on sustainability reporting. The study recommends that Nigerian banks should strengthen audit committees by appointing members with strong financial and accounting expertise. Similarly, Regulators should promote gender diversity and encourage women leadership among the audit committee to improve inclusivity and ethical governance.

title: Strategic Leadership and Organizational Agility of Micro Start-Up Enterprises in Region XII Towards Industry 4.0 Readiness
summary: This study assessed the Industry 4.0 preparedness of micro start-up enterprises in Region XII (SOCCSKSARGEN) with a focus on strategic leadership and organizational agility. Based on Strategic Leadership Theory, Dynamic Capabilities Theory and the Industry 4.0 Readiness Model, the study investigated organizational capabilities that enable firms to respond to technological and market changes. The study employed a quantitative descriptive-correlational research design involving micro start-up enterprises in the region. The respondents were owners, co-founders or managers and data was collected through structured questionnaires. The levels of strategic leadership, organizational agility and Industry 4.0 readiness were determined through descriptive statistics, tests of significant differences and multiple regression analysis to examine the predictive contribution of the organizational variables. The results showed that strategic leadership and organizational agility were Highly Practiced, and Industry 4.0 readiness was Moderately Ready. Environmental Scanning was relatively a lower dimension of strategic leadership while flexibility and operational speed was relatively a lower dimension of organizational agility. Least mature dimension of Industry 4.0 readiness was Data-Driven Decision Making. Regression analysis showed that organizational agility significantly predicted Industry 4.0 readiness, but strategic leadership did not make a significant unique contribution when both variables were considered simultaneously. Based on these findings, the Strategic Agility and Industry 4.0 Readiness Enhancement (SAIRE) Framework was proposed to strengthen environmental scanning, leadership capability, organizational flexibility, operational speed, digital transformation and data-driven decision making, thus improving competitiveness, innovation, resilience and sustainable development.

title: COLLABORATIVE INNOVATION MODELS FOR APPLICATION-ORIENTED MARITIME UNDERGRADUATE COLLEGES UNDER THE BACKGROUND OF BUILDING A MARITIME POWER
summary: Building a maritime power is a talent problem before it is a technology problem, and application-oriented maritime undergraduate colleges sit where the two meet. Their inherited teaching models, though, were designed for a shipping industry that no longer exists, and the distance between what they produce and what the blue economy needs has widened under digital transformation. This paper asks what collaborative innovation actually looks like inside such institutions, and whether the multi-stakeholder arrangements now promoted in Chinese policy close that distance. The study is qualitative. It works through the Triple Helix and Quadruple Helix literatures, reads the relevant policy texts, and then examines three Chinese institutions in detail (Jimei University, Dalian Maritime University, and Jiangsu University of Science and Technology). Four arrangements recur across the cases: government-university-industry-research synergies, industry-education integration platforms, project-based training mechanisms, and ecosystems built around digital intelligence. Where these are in place, graduates match employer requirements more closely and maritime technologies reach commercial use faster. Cross-sector partnership needs institutionalizing rather than improvising, and digital infrastructure should be treated as shared equipment rather than as a departmental purchase. Without both, maritime higher education will go on describing itself as a servant of national strategy while lagging behind it.

title: Confirmatory Factor Analysis of an Innovative Leadership Model for Private Universities in Hainan
summary: Purpose: This study examined and quantitatively validated an innovative leadership model for administrators of private universities in Hainan Province, China, in response to increasing demands for organizational innovation and digital transformation within the Hainan Free Trade Port context. Research design, data and methodology: The study reports the quantitative phase of a broader research project on innovative leadership. Preliminary variables were identified and refined through literature review and structured interviews in the first qualitative phase. In the present phase, quantitative data were collected from 429 faculty members using a 48-item questionnaire. Exploratory factor analysis and second-order confirmatory factor analysis were employed, with 45 retained items aggregated into 15 composite indicators for examine the factor structure and validate the proposed model. Results: The results initially supported 16 innovative leadership variables. One variable, Models Learning, was removed because of weak factor loadings in the exploratory factor analysis. The remaining variables were organized into five dimensions: Supportive Organizational Environment, Digital Connectivity, Innovative Capability, Collaborative Team Culture, and Innovative Strategic Orientation. Conclusions: The findings suggest that innovative leadership in private universities is a multidimensional construct. The validated model provides a context-specific structure for understanding and assessing innovative leadership among administrators in private universities in Hainan Province.

title: Beyond the Liability of Origin: Multidimensional Legitimacy and ESG Strategies of Emerging Market Multinationals
summary: ABSTRACT Drawing on a multidimensional legitimacy perspective, this study examines how internationalization shapes the ESG performance of emerging market multinational enterprises (EMNEs). EMNEs face not only external legitimacy pressures in host‐country markets but also internal legitimacy pressures in the home‐country institutional environment. These internal pressures are especially salient for state‐owned EMNEs because of their stronger political embeddedness and closer alignment with state priorities. Using panel data on 16,342 firm‐year observations from Chinese listed firms covering 2009–2022, the findings show that greater geographic breadth of internationalization is positively associated with ESG performance. This relationship is stronger for state‐owned EMNEs, suggesting that their ESG strategies are shaped by the need to maintain legitimacy both abroad and at home. Board overseas experience further strengthens this effect, indicating that internationally experienced directors help firms reconcile competing home‐ and host‐country expectations during international expansion. By integrating external and internal legitimacy into the analysis of EMNE ESG strategies, this study extends research on internationalization, legitimacy, and corporate governance and highlights the role of board‐level international experience in translating legitimacy pressures into stronger ESG engagement.

title: Innovative Frontiers in Commerce: Emerging Trends and Future Opportunities
summary: Abstract The rapid advancement of technology, changing consumer preferences, and increasing global interconnectedness are transforming the traditional landscape of commerce. This research paper examines the innovative frontiers shaping modern commerce, with particular emphasis on emerging technologies, digital transformation, evolving business models, and changing consumer behaviour. Technologies such as artificial intelligence, blockchain, big data analytics, cloud computing, automation, and digital payment systems are creating new opportunities for businesses to improve operational efficiency, enhance customer experiences, and expand their market reach. The study also explores the growing significance of e-commerce, social commerce, omnichannel retailing, and sustainable business practices in shaping the future of commercial activities. Alongside these opportunities, businesses face challenges related to cybersecurity, data privacy, technological adoption, regulatory uncertainty, and the need for continuous innovation. The paper highlights how organizations can adapt to these developments by embracing technology-driven strategies, fostering innovation, and responding effectively to changing market demands. The study concludes that the future of commerce will be characterized by greater digital integration, personalization, sustainability, and technology-enabled business ecosystems. Understanding these emerging trends is essential for businesses, policymakers, researchers, and other stakeholders seeking to navigate the evolving commercial environment and capitalize on future opportunities.
